finding.description: Describes a defect in the same-role review, not a candidate defect already captured by a supported review finding.

reviewFindingAdjudication.description: Judges one finding made by the same-role review rather than judging the candidate defect again.

findingIds.description: Links only adjudicator findings that explain why this review finding is rejected; this array is empty when judgment is supported.

surfaceAdjudication.description: Echoes the bound same-role review assessment in reviewAssessmentJudgment and judges the soundness of that assessment in judgment. A sound blocking review assessment is blocking plus supported, not an adjudication failure.

findingIds.description: Links only adjudicator findings that explain a rejected same-role review assessment. It is empty for supported; rejected requires a linked blocking finding on this surface.

judgment.description: supported approves the same-role review assessment even when reviewAssessmentJudgment is blocking; rejected means the assessment is unsound or incomplete.

reviewAssessmentJudgment.description: Exact echo of the bound same-role review assessment's judgment; the deterministic verifier rejects any mismatch.

adjudicationSchema.description: This record judges the soundness and completeness of the same-role review, not the candidate.

findings.description: Adjudicator findings describe defects in the same-role review's requirement, assessment, reasoning, finding, coverage, or severity; they do not repeat candidate defects already captured by supported review findings.

reviewFindingAdjudications.description: Each entry judges one same-role review finding. A supported review finding has no adjudicator-finding links; a rejected review finding requires a linked blocking adjudicator finding that explains the review defect.

surfaceAdjudications.description: Each entry exactly echoes the same-role review assessment's pass, advisory, or blocking judgment, then separately judges that assessment as supported or rejected; it does not judge the candidate surface directly.

verdict.description: pass means the same-role review is sound and complete, even when that review correctly fails the candidate; fail means the same-role review is unsound or incomplete. This verdict never judges the candidate directly.

adjudicationSchema.title: Independent canonical-English semantic adjudication record

adjudicationSemantics.failMeaning: The same-role review is unsound or incomplete.
adjudicationSemantics.findingLinkMeaning: A supported surface assessment or review finding has no adjudicator-finding links; a rejected one links at least one blocking adjudicator finding on an overlapping surface that explains a defect in the review.
adjudicationSemantics.passMeaning: The same-role review is sound and complete, even when that review correctly fails the candidate.
adjudicationSemantics.subject: same-role-review
adjudicationSemantics.surfaceAdjudicationMeaning: Each surface adjudication exactly echoes the bound review assessment judgment in reviewAssessmentJudgment, then uses judgment supported or rejected to judge that assessment.

From text to a working model

Follow small, executable examples until tensors, attention, training, and generation fit together as one Rust program.

LLM from scratch

Build the parts of a small language model in Rust, from tokenization to training and generation. Chapters 0–39.

Practical LLM in Rust

Extend the completed model with corpus preparation, efficient execution, and measured training and inference. Start with the course structure in Chapter 0.

Connect code to the formula

See what came before

<aside class="lesson-objective"> <strong>In this chapter</strong> <p>Understand the practical course's starting implementation, prerequisites and chapter sequence, and distinguish small examples from larger measured runs.</p> </aside>  </header> <div class="lesson-body"> 
<h2 id="start-from-a-working-model">Start from a working model</h2>
<p>This course starts from a working language model and studies what must change as
the data, model and workload grow. The starting implementation is a separate
copy of the model completed in <em>LLM from scratch</em>. It already contains byte-pair
tokenization, tensors, automatic differentiation, a causal decoder, training,
evaluation, checkpoints and cached generation. Here we extend those parts.</p>
<p>Chapter 0 is an orientation. Chapter 1 begins the learning material by recording
exactly what the small reference model demonstrates. That record gives later
changes a concrete comparison point.</p>
<h2 id="before-starting">Before starting</h2>
<p>Complete <a href="/en/course/">LLM from scratch</a> or bring equivalent experience with
Rust, byte-pair encoding, causal attention, gradients and next-token training.
The first course’s <a href="/en/course/39-end-to-end-llm/">Chapter 39</a> shows the complete
small model. Familiarity with that model matters more than memorizing its
chapter numbers.</p>
<p>The initial reference and Rust loading of an already prepared corpus run on a
CPU. The GPU-backed practical path requires a compatible NVIDIA GPU. The external
corpus-preparation example uses NVIDIA NeMo Curator and needs a GPU and driver
compatible with its pinned CUDA/RAPIDS environment. NeMo prepares text outside
the Rust model; another tool can supply the same prepared-document format.</p>

<h2 id="keep-the-completed-model-as-the-starting-point">Keep the completed model as the starting point</h2>
<p>The first course builds the mechanisms of a small causal language model. This
course begins with its completed implementation and studies how data handling,
execution, training and inference must change for larger workloads. The Rust
implementation for this course lives in
<code>rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical</code>. Its examples extend that copy; the first
course keeps its own implementation.</p>

<h2 id="follow-the-practical-path">Follow the practical path</h2>
<ol>
<li><a href="../01-reference-core-handoff/">Chapter 1: Record the reference model</a> binds
the tiny experiment to its inputs and separates repeatable results from
claims about language quality or speed.</li>
<li><a href="../02-corpus-preparation/">Chapter 2: Prepare a corpus</a> separates external
text preparation from Rust loading, and preserves document and split identity.</li>
<li><a href="../03-scalable-bpe-tokenizer/">Chapter 3</a> extends byte-pair encoding. It adds
bounded ingestion, local pair updates and efficient application of frozen
merge ranks to the existing tokenizer.</li>
</ol>
<p>The <a href="/en/practical-llm-in-rust/">practical course index</a> links to the lessons
currently available. The later curriculum continues with variable-length batches and packing,
configurable decoder depth and shape, GPU execution, larger training runs,
complete resume state, evaluation, adaptation, quantized inference and serving.
These are stages of one causal text model. Their examples become available as
each mechanism is implemented and measured.</p>
<h2 id="read-the-examples-at-their-stated-scale">Read the examples at their stated scale</h2>
<p>Small fixtures make intermediate values inspectable: a pair count, a token
sequence, a loss or a restored state. They establish the behavior shown for
those inputs. They do not establish full-corpus throughput, useful generated
language, or a larger model’s memory use. Full-data runs and hardware
measurements supply that separate evidence.</p>

<h2 id="use-the-sequence-to-navigate">Use the sequence to navigate</h2>
<p>An ordered chapter list connects each available lesson to its purpose and names
the later stages. The individual lessons introduce diagrams where a computation
or comparison benefits from one.</p>

<h2 id="continue-with-the-reference-experiment">Continue with the reference experiment</h2>
<p>Corpus preparation and tokenization supply the causal decoder’s inputs. Later
chapters change how that same model is configured, trained, evaluated and used
for generation. Start by establishing the reference experiment in
<a href="../01-reference-core-handoff/">Chapter 1</a>.</p> </div> <nav class="chapter-navigation" aria-label="Chapter navigation" data-chapter-navigation data-astro-cid-44eis63d>  <a <h2 id="the-problem-changes-need-a-fixed-comparison-point">The problem: changes need a fixed comparison point</h2>
<p>The final chapter of <em>LLM from scratch</em> joined the tokenizer, decoder, training,
evaluation, checkpoint and generation code. This practical course starts from a
separate copy of that implementation. If the
data, configuration and code change together, a changed result no longer tells
you which version you observed. You need a fixed reference that identifies its
inputs and states exactly what its checks establish.</p>
<p>This chapter runs the completed first-course pipeline without modifying it. The
practical copy can then evolve while this comparison point stays fixed. The example gives that reference
an input identity and a report whose claims stay attached to their evidence.
The identity identifies the fixed inputs. The checks establish which behavior
this execution reproduced. Neither establishes useful laptop-scale capability.</p>

<p>The example verifies its compiled reference-source evidence first. It then
rejects changed corpus or split bytes before training or checkpoint work.
Only accepted fixed inputs reach the existing pipeline. The wrapper calls that
pipeline once; the pipeline itself performs primary training and replay.</p>

<h3 id="what-matching-identities-do-not-prove">What matching identities do not prove</h3>
<p>A matching digest identifies the same canonical input record, subject to the
hash’s collision-resistance assumption. It does not prove that the algorithm
is correct or that a new machine will reproduce every floating-point bit.</p>
<p>The source identity deliberately covers the forty first-course source files,
not the evolving practical crate, this chapter’s reporting wrapper or interface. Toolchain, locked
dependencies and arithmetic environment are recorded separately. A matching
source digest is therefore not evidence that two execution environments match.
The temporary checkpoint path is also outside the input identity; changing
that path does not change the model’s fixed inputs.</p>
<p>Likewise, exact checkpoint reload is narrower than complete job resumption.
This check does not restore every data cursor, in-flight operation or whole-job
continuation state. No laptop throughput is measured here.</p>

<h2 id="history-reporting-conditions-and-measuring-variation">History: reporting conditions and measuring variation</h2>
<p>A language-model score without its input conditions and scope does not identify
what was evaluated or establish which capabilities were checked.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03993v2">Model Cards for Model Reporting</a> was
presented in 2019. Mitchell and colleagues propose model documentation that
includes intended uses and evaluation conditions; a model card is not itself
proof of quality.</p>
<p>Model Cards describe evaluation conditions and intended uses; later fine-tuning
experiments study variation across initializations and data orders. Reporting
scope and measuring variation answer different questions.</p>
<p>In <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.06305v1">Fine-Tuning Pretrained Language Models: Weight Initializations, Data Orders, and Early Stopping</a>,
published in 2020, Dodge and colleagues study fine-tuning variability associated
with initialization and data order for pretrained language models. This does
not measure variability in the course’s tiny decoder.</p>
<p>Keep a fixed regression reference when changing an LLM pipeline, while recording
separately the evidence needed for quality, seed sensitivity and hardware claims.</p>
<p>The Rust reporting contrast uses the same observation. Reading only the mean
NLL with this expression gives a number:</p>

accounting and limits. It does not retrain a historical model or execute a seed

<h2 id="keep-the-three-evidence-layers-separate">Keep the three evidence layers separate</h2>
<p>The digest identifies the fixed inputs. The counts and generated token IDs
describe checked behavior on those inputs. The final card keeps future quality,
job-resumption and hardware claims outside the reference’s evidence boundary.</p>

Separate checks observe replay, fixed-window evaluation, reload and cached generation. <h2 id="optional-practice-inspect-the-boundary">Optional practice: inspect the boundary</h2>
<p>From the repository root, with Docker and the Rust/site course image available,
run the example and inspect its JSON report:</p>
<pre class="astro-code github-dark-high-contrast" style="background-color:#0a0c10;color:#f0f3f6;overflow-x:auto" tabindex="0" data-language="sh" dir="ltr"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#F0F3F6">COURSE_CORPUS</span><span style="color:#FF9492">=</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF">false</span><span style="color:#FFB757"> ./course</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> run</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> cargo</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> run</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --quiet</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --offline</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --locked</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> -p</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> practical-ch01-reference-core-handoff</span></span></code></pre>
<p>The output contains the fixed input identity and the checked scalar-reference
observations described in this chapter.</p>
<ol>
<li>
<p>In the JSON report printed by the Chapter 1 reference example, find the input
identity, target-count basis and metric unit. Explain why a digest alone would
not replace the replay and reload checks.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Run the pure identity-input mutation test. Identify its changes to configuration,
corpus, split bytes and source identity without training. Explain why constructing
an identity for changed inputs does not admit them to the fixed reference run.</p>
<p>From the repository root, with Docker and the Rust/site course image available,
run:</p>
<pre class="astro-code github-dark-high-contrast" style="background-color:#0a0c10;color:#f0f3f6;overflow-x:auto" tabindex="0" data-language="sh" dir="ltr"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#F0F3F6">COURSE_CORPUS</span><span style="color:#FF9492">=</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF">false</span><span style="color:#FFB757"> ./course</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> run</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> cargo</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> test</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --offline</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --locked</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> -p</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> practical-ch01-reference-core-handoff</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --test</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> reference_handoff</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> every_identity_input_is_bound_without_training</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --exact</span></span></code></pre>
<p>Expected result: one selected test passes. A zero-test result does not
reproduce this check.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Explain why a successful checkpoint round trip cannot justify the statement
“the complete training job can resume,” and why <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1744</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1744</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1744</span></span></span></span> must not be labeled
“distinct test transitions.”</p>
</li>
</ol>
<details><summary>Answers: input identity, evidence scope and repeated target slots</summary><ol>
<li>The digest binds inputs; replay and reload compare actual behavior. Neither
kind of evidence substitutes for the other. The target-count basis explicitly
derives <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2048</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2048</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2048</span></span></span></span> targets per schedule and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>4096</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4096</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">4096</span></span></span></span> for primary plus replay.
The reported mean NLL uses nats per overlapping window-target slot.</li>
<li>The pure mutation test constructs different identities without calling the
pipeline. The runner separately requires the exact accepted corpus and split
bytes, so an identity is not an admission permit.</li>
<li>The checkpoint check covers persisted model, optimizer and tokenizer state
plus a fixed logit probe, not every whole-job continuation dependency. The
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1744</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1744</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1744</span></span></span></span> denominator counts overlapping window-target slots; the underlying
documents contain <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>442</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">442</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">442</span></span></span></span> transition occurrences.</li>
</ol></details>

input identity and evidence. Chapter 2 uses NVIDIA NeMo Curator to prepare
supplied text, then loads the prepared documents through the practical crate’s
Rust reader.

<h2 id="the-problem-the-model-learns-from-the-text-we-let-through">The problem: the model learns from the text we let through</h2>
<p>A language model learns to predict tokens from the documents supplied during
training. Its optimizer does not decide whether those documents are appropriate
for the task, whether we may use them, or whether a purportedly unseen test
example also appears in the training input. Those decisions must happen before
training.</p>
<p>Repeated text creates another problem. If one training pass visits every stored
document occurrence, each copy of a document supplies another copy of its token
targets. The repeated text receives more influence without adding new examples.
Removing duplicates changes that weighting; it does not merely save disk space.</p>
<p>Corpus preparation therefore has two outputs: selected text and evidence about
how it was selected. We need source context, declared exclusion rules, duplicate
handling and protected evaluation boundaries. A large file or a successful
download supplies none of those conclusions on its own.</p>
<p>We will use <a href="https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/curator/v26.07/curate-text">NVIDIA NeMo Curator</a>
to prepare text. It is an external tool, not
part of the Rust language model, and another preparation tool can replace it if
it produces the same documented input for the model. Rust will only load the
prepared documents. The extended tokenizer in Chapter 3 will then learn from the
training documents, not the validation or test documents.</p>
<h2 id="the-solution-prepare-documents-then-load-a-stable-format">The solution: prepare documents, then load a stable format</h2>
<p>Keep one document as one record throughout the preparation pipeline. Retain a
stable document ID and the source information needed to trace that record. A
source record should identify where the text came from, its revision and the
applicable license and attribution. A checksum identifies selected bytes; it
does not establish permission to use those bytes or tell us what they contain.</p>
<p>Apply declared quality rules, inspect what those rules exclude, and handle
duplicates before final training input is frozen. Quality rules are proxies:
for example, a minimum word count rejects short records, not every unsuitable
record. A rule can also remove useful text. Inspect both survivors and exclusions
rather than interpreting a low exclusion rate as success.</p>
<p>Keep privacy review separate from quality scoring. Passing a word-count filter
or removing duplicates does not remove names, addresses, credentials or other
sensitive content. Withhold unresolved records from training; do not copy their
sensitive text into public reports. Retain enough source and transformation
information to identify affected derived corpora if an input is withdrawn.
Removing a source from a later corpus does not erase what an already trained
model may have learned from it.</p>
<h3 id="a-six-document-example">A six-document example</h3>
<p>The practical example uses course-authored text, not a result for a large
training corpus. Its JSONL input contains these six documents:</p>















































<table><thead><tr><th>Document ID</th><th>Text</th><th>Source group</th><th>Relevant observation</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>story-a</code></td><td>A cat naps.</td><td><code>family-a</code></td><td>Three words</td></tr><tr><td><code>story-b</code></td><td>A cat naps.</td><td><code>family-a</code></td><td>An identical copy of <code>story-a</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>story-c</code></td><td>A dog runs.</td><td><code>family-b</code></td><td>Three words</td></tr><tr><td><code>story-d</code></td><td>Rain feeds trees.</td><td><code>family-c</code></td><td>Three words</td></tr><tr><td><code>story-e</code></td><td>hi</td><td><code>family-e</code></td><td>One word</td></tr><tr><td><code>story-f</code></td><td>!!!</td><td><code>family-f</code></td><td>Punctuation only</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>Configure NeMo’s word-count filter to retain records with at least <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">3</span></span></span></span> and at
most <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">20</span></span></span></span> words. Its English setting counts whitespace-separated items; that
proxy is not a linguistic definition of a word. The <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">4</span></span></span></span> story occurrences
survive; <code>hi</code> and the punctuation-only
record do not. Exact duplicate removal then leaves <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">3</span></span></span></span> distinct story texts.
The punctuation-only record has one whitespace-separated item too; this
particular rule rejects it for length, not because it recognizes punctuation
as unsuitable language-model training text.
The duplicate-removal workflow may retain either cat-story ID; the result we
care about here is one cat-story occurrence, not a promised representative ID
or output-file order.</p>
<p>Before deduplication, the cat story occupies <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span> of the <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">4</span></span></span></span> surviving document
occurrences. After deduplication, it occupies <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span> of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">3</span></span></span></span> distinct documents. Under
uniform sampling of these whole-stage document occurrences before separating
their roles, its selection probability would change from <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2/4</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">2/4</span></span></span></span> to <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/3</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">1/3</span></span></span></span>.
That calculation illustrates duplicate weighting, not a sampler used to train
on this fixture. Actual token-target weighting also depends on document length,
split selection and the batching policy; document fractions are not token
fractions.</p>
<p>NeMo’s exact method groups hashes of text and identifies copies to remove.
It does not identify paraphrases, and hash grouping is not an adversarial
collision-proof comparison. NeMo’s fuzzy method uses approximate similarity
search for near-duplicates. Its configuration trades missed matches against
unwanted matches; it does not certify a universal similarity cutoff or detect
all ways an evaluation example could have leaked into training.</p>
<h3 id="freeze-the-roles-of-the-prepared-documents">Freeze the roles of the prepared documents</h3>
<p>The training split supplies examples for fitting the tokenizer and model.
The validation split supplies examples for selecting settings or deciding when
to stop training. The test split is reserved for final evaluation. Do not move
a difficult held-out document into training after seeing its score.</p>
<p>Related records must not be scattered across those roles. Treat an identified
duplicate family or other known related source group as one unit when assigning
splits. Otherwise two different IDs can put substantially the same example in
both training and evaluation. For this fixture, the two cat-story copies share
<code>family-a</code>; their different IDs do not make them independent examples.</p>
<p>For the exercise, a supplied policy assigns <code>family-a</code>, <code>family-e</code> and
<code>family-f</code> to training, <code>family-b</code> to validation and <code>family-c</code> to test. We fix
that policy before running the filters. Both cat-story copies therefore have
the same role regardless of which ID duplicate removal keeps. The prepared
fixture has one document in each role: the cat story in training, the dog story
in validation and the rain story in test.</p>
<p>The recipe uses Pandas to join those declared assignments to the source-group
metadata. It refuses an unassigned group rather than choosing a convenient role
after seeing the output. This checks the supplied groups, not whether we have
discovered every related pair. One held-out story is also far too little
evidence for a meaningful model-quality estimate.</p>
<p>Split disjointness and decontamination are different checks. Disjoint IDs do not
prove different text. Removing exact duplicates does not prove that near-copies
or external benchmark examples are absent. Declare the protected evaluation
material and the overlap method before inspecting results, report its measured
scope, and keep unresolved overlaps out of training. A check against a named
evaluation set does not establish internet-wide contamination freedom.</p>
<h3 id="export-documents-not-preparation-specific-objects">Export documents, not preparation-specific objects</h3>
<p>The handoff to Rust is UTF-8 <strong>JSON Lines</strong>: one JSON object per physical line.
Each object has a nonblank string <code>id</code> and a nonblank string <code>text</code>. Other fields
are retained as metadata. For example:</p>
<pre class="astro-code github-dark-high-contrast" style="background-color:#0a0c10;color:#f0f3f6;overflow-x:auto" tabindex="0" data-language="json" dir="ltr"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#F0F3F6">{</span><span style="color:#72F088">"id"</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">:</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF">"story-c"</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">,</span><span style="color:#72F088">"text"</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">:</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF">"A dog runs."</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">,</span><span style="color:#72F088">"source_group"</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">:</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF">"family-b"</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">}</span></span></code></pre>
<p>The document ID is a label, not a token ID or a required filename. The text is
still text; tokenization comes next. A newline inside document text must be
escaped as <code>\n</code> inside the JSON string, so it does not create a second record.
Source and split records remain linked to the exported documents, but a JSONL
file alone does not certify that those decisions were made correctly.</p>

<h2 id="practical-preparation-with-nemo-curator">Practical preparation with NeMo Curator</h2>
<p>This workflow uses a separately built NeMo Curator image. You need Linux,
Docker, a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver, and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit so
Docker can expose the GPU. The pinned NeMo release must be compatible with that
CUDA/driver stack. Rust’s prepared-corpus reader does not require a GPU or CUDA.</p>
<p>Run the following commands from the repository root. The image build may use
network access to obtain the external tool. It does not acquire a training
corpus or add NeMo to the Rust/site image:</p>
<pre class="astro-code github-dark-high-contrast" style="background-color:#0a0c10;color:#f0f3f6;overflow-x:auto" tabindex="0" data-language="sh" dir="ltr"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#FFB757">docker</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> build</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --file</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> docker/nemo-curator.Dockerfile</span><span style="color:#FF9492"> \</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#91CBFF">  --tag</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> learn-llm-nemo-curator:26.07</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> .</span></span></code></pre>
<p>With the NeMo image built and the NVIDIA GPU available to Docker, run from the
repository root. Create a fresh output directory for the exercise, then run the
tool with network access disabled. The read-only mount supplies the recipe and
its six-record fixture; the writable mount receives generated preparation output:</p>
<pre class="astro-code github-dark-high-contrast" style="background-color:#0a0c10;color:#f0f3f6;overflow-x:auto" tabindex="0" data-language="sh" dir="ltr"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#FFB757">mkdir</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> -p</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#FFB757">docker</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> run</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --rm</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --network</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> none</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --gpus</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> all</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --memory=8g</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --cpus=2</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --shm-size=1g</span><span style="color:#FF9492"> \</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#91CBFF">  --hostname</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> course-nemo</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --add-host</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> course-nemo:127.0.0.1</span><span style="color:#FF9492"> \</span></span>

<p>The recipe invokes NeMo’s reader, configured word-count filter, exact duplicate

<h2 id="load-the-prepared-output-in-rust">Load the prepared output in Rust</h2>
<p><code>PreparedCorpusReader</code> accepts any caller-supplied <code>BufRead</code> stream. A file,
memory buffer or database export can supply that stream without changing the
loader. Standard buffered I/O reads physical lines; Serde JSON parses their
objects. The loader preserves decoded text and metadata. It does not normalize
text, reject duplicate content or assign a split.</p>
<figure class="rust-source" data-source-path="rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs" data-source-region="prepared-document-json" data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5> <figcaption data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5> <span data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5>The prepared-corpus loader uses Serde JSON to decode required document fields, then rejects blank IDs or text without rewriting their content.</span> <code dir="ltr" data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5>rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs#prepared-document-json</code> </figcaption> <pre class="astro-code github-dark-high-contrast rust-source-code" style="background-color:#0a0c10;color:#f0f3f6; overflow-x: auto;" tabindex="0" aria-label="Rust source: decode one prepared document without curating it" dir="ltr" data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5 data-language="rust"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#FF9492">        let</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6"> document</span><span style="color:#FF9492">:</span><span style="color:#FFB757"> PreparedDocument</span><span style="color:#FF9492"> =</span><span style="color:#FFB757"> serde_json</span><span style="color:#FF9492">::</span><span style="color:#DBB7FF">from_slice</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">(</span><span style="color:#FF9492">&</span><span style="color:#91CBFF">self</span><span style="color:#FF9492">.</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">buffer)</span></span>

<span class="line"><span style="color:#FF9492">        for</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6"> (field, value) </span><span style="color:#FF9492">in</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6"> [(</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF">"id"</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">, </span><span style="color:#FF9492">&</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">document</span><span style="color:#FF9492">.</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">id), (</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF">"text"</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">, </span><span style="color:#FF9492">&</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">document</span><span style="color:#FF9492">.</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">text)] {</span></span>

<span class="line"><span style="color:#FF9492">                return</span><span style="color:#FFB757"> Err</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">(</span><span style="color:#FFB757">CorpusReadError</span><span style="color:#FF9492">::</span><span style="color:#FFB757">EmptyField</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6"> { line, field });</span></span>

<span class="line"><span style="color:#F0F3F6">        }</span></span></code></pre> </figure>
<p>The caller chooses maximum source-record bytes, document count and cumulative
decoded-text bytes. Record bytes include the physical line ending; decoded text
bytes count the UTF-8 representation of the <code>text</code> value, not JSON syntax or
metadata. An oversized record, malformed JSON, missing required field, failed
read or exceeded limit stops the stream with an error. No failed document is
returned or counted. Documents returned earlier are not rolled back.</p>

<p>The demo reads standard input, retains only the first three document descriptions
for its summary, and emits that summary only after the complete input succeeds.
It can therefore inspect a large stream without retaining every text. This is
not a transactional storage adapter: a caller storing documents as they arrive
must provide its own staging if partial results must stay unpublished.</p>

<h2 id="history-more-text-was-not-the-whole-solution">History: more text was not the whole solution</h2>
<p>Collecting readable text alone does not document its intended use, control the
weight of repeated occurrences or protect held-out evaluation from training
overlap.</p>
<p>Dataset documentation makes source context reviewable; deduplication studies
connect repeated training text with memorization and train-test overlap in
their measured settings.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09010v8">Datasheets for Datasets</a> was first posted in
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2018</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2018</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2018</span></span></span></span>. Gebru and colleagues propose documenting dataset motivation,
composition, collection and intended uses so those choices can be reviewed.
Documentation records context; it does not itself establish permission or
privacy.</p>
<p>The <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2021</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2021</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2021</span></span></span></span> <a href="https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.98/">C4 analysis</a> examined
where web-corpus text came from and what filtering removed. Its finding that
blocklist filtering disproportionately excluded text from and about minority
individuals is a reason to inspect exclusions, not to label every filter neutral.</p>
<p>In <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2022</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2022</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2022</span></span></span></span>, <a href="https://aclanthology.org/2022.acl-long.577/">Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better</a>
studied duplicate handling in training corpora. Lee and colleagues report reduced memorized output and train-test
overlap after deduplication in their studied corpora and models; those outcomes
are not measurements of this course fixture. They explain why duplicate
handling and evaluation separation matter in addition to collecting and
documenting text.</p>
<p>The following Rust comparison loads two identical supplied records and keeps
both. It illustrates the limitation of merely reading raw occurrences, not a
reimplementation of those studies’ preparation tools:</p>
<figure class="rust-source" data-source-path="rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs" data-source-region="loading-is-not-preparation" data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5> <figcaption data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5> <span data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5>Reading two identical JSONL records returns two documents; the loader does not silently perform duplicate removal.</span> <code dir="ltr" data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5>rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs#loading-is-not-preparation</code> </figcaption> <pre class="astro-code github-dark-high-contrast rust-source-code" style="background-color:#0a0c10;color:#f0f3f6; overflow-x: auto;" tabindex="0" aria-label="Rust comparison: loading records does not prepare a corpus" dir="ltr" data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5 data-language="rust"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#F0F3F6">    #[test]</span></span>

<span class="line"><span style="color:#FF9492">        let</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6"> source </span><span style="color:#FF9492">=</span></span>

<span class="line"><span style="color:#F0F3F6">    }</span></span></code></pre> </figure>
<p>Keep documented source and selection evidence, inspect exclusions, handle
related records together and preserve held-out roles before tokenizer learning
or model training. No single preparation statistic certifies suitability.</p>

<h2 id="what-reaches-the-language-model-next">What reaches the language model next</h2>
<p>Prepared training documents become the tokenizer’s learning input in Chapter 3.
Held-out documents may be encoded with the learned tokenizer, but they must not
change its learned vocabulary or merge choices. Later batching creates token
targets from that same frozen training selection. NeMo has not implemented any
of those Rust LLM algorithms; it has supplied documented text for them to learn

<h2 id="the-problem-repeated-scans-must-not-change-learned-choices">The problem: repeated scans must not change learned choices</h2>
<p>Our byte-pair encoding trainer counts adjacent token pairs, selects one pair,
replaces its occurrences and repeats. The first course’s
<a href="/en/course/03-learn-bpe-merges/">Chapter 3</a> implemented that scalar trainer;
<a href="/en/course/04-apply-bpe-tokenizer/">Chapter 4</a> applied its frozen ranks and
decoded the resulting tokens. Both are already in the practical course’s
starting crate. Here we extend the existing <code>BpeTrainer</code> and <code>BpeTokenizer</code>.</p>
<p>The scalar trainer recounts every current training sequence at every merge
rank. With more documents and
more requested merges, those repeated scans revisit many edges that have not
changed.</p>
<p>We can retain pair statistics and update the edges affected by a replacement.
Local updates avoid recounting unaffected edges, but introduce a correctness obligation:
the retained counts must describe the current sequences exactly. An old count
or an out-of-order replacement can change the learned vocabulary even if the
result still decodes to the original bytes.</p>
<p>We will preserve the course’s policy: learn from training documents only, count
overlapping adjacent occurrences, break frequency ties by numeric token IDs,
and replace matches left to right without sharing an input token between two
replacements. A faster implementation of that policy must keep those decisions.</p>
<h3 id="work-through-two-merge-ranks">Work through two merge ranks</h3>
<p>Use two manually prepared training documents, <code>abab</code> and <code>abac</code>. They are
separate documents, so the last byte of one never forms a pair with the first
byte of the other. The held-out text <code>acac</code> will be encoded after learning;
it supplies no pair counts.</p>
<p>Keep the existing public token layout. Program IDs <code>0</code> and <code>1</code> are BOS and EOS;
one-byte content IDs run from <code>2</code> through <code>257</code>. The bytes <code>a</code>, <code>b</code> and <code>c</code>
therefore have IDs <code>99</code>, <code>100</code> and <code>101</code>. The first learned content ID is <code>258</code>.
There is no PAD token. BOS and EOS are structural controls and do not enter
training pair counts.</p>
<p>Before rank <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span>, the current sequences are <code>[99,100,99,100]</code> and
<code>[99,100,99,101]</code>. The pair <code>a,b</code> occurs <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">3</span></span></span></span> times, <code>b,a</code> occurs <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span> times, and
<code>a,c</code> occurs once. Select <code>a,b</code>, assign its merged bytes <code>ab</code> the new ID <code>258</code>,
and replace its nonoverlapping occurrences. The sequences become <code>[258,258]</code>
and <code>[258,99,101]</code>.</p>
<p>Before rank <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span>, there are only three adjacent occurrences: <code>(258,258)</code>,
<code>(258,99)</code> and <code>(99,101)</code>, each with count <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span>. Numeric pair order compares
the left IDs first. The pair <code>(99,101)</code> wins the tie, so the bytes <code>ac</code> receive
ID <code>259</code>. The two training sequences are now <code>[258,258]</code> and <code>[258,259]</code>.</p>
<p>The frozen rules encode held-out <code>acac</code> as <code>[259,259]</code>. Decoding those content
tokens reconstructs <code>acac</code>; document framing would instead give
<code>[0,259,259,1]</code>. Encoding held-out text applies the learned rules and does not
learn another rule.</p>

<p>First collect all pairs having the largest current count. Then choose the
numerically smallest pair from that set: smallest left ID, then smallest right
ID. If there are no adjacent pairs, learning stops. The prepared-training policy
can require an exact merge count. With that policy enabled, training fails if
the documents run out of pairs before that count is reached; it does not invent
vocabulary entries. Without it, the requested count is an upper limit, as in
the original scalar trainer.</p>

<h2 id="what-the-symbols-count">What the symbols count</h2>
<ul>
<li><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6151em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">t</span></span></span></span> is the zero-based merge rank, counting completed earlier merge rounds.</li>
<li><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a,b</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8889em;vertical-align:-0.1944em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">a</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">b</span></span></span></span> are the left and right content token IDs of an adjacent pair in a current
training document.</li>
<li><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_t(a,b)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">c</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.2806em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:0em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">t</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">a</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">b</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span> is the integer number of adjacent occurrences of that pair in the
current training sequences at rank <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6151em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">t</span></span></span></span>; overlaps count and document boundaries
never contribute.</li>
<li><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_t</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.625em;vertical-align:-0.1944em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.2806em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:0em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">t</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> is the selected pair: maximum current count, with ties resolved by the
smallest left ID and then the smallest right ID.</li>
</ul>
<p>For <code>aaa</code>, two overlapping <code>a,a</code> occurrences contribute to the count, but
left-to-right replacement consumes the first two bytes together and leaves the
third byte alone. That produces one replacement. For <code>aaaa</code>, three occurrences
contribute to the count and two nonoverlapping replacements are possible.
Frequency and replacement count answer different questions.</p>

<h2 id="keep-live-edges-then-apply-learned-ranks">Keep live edges, then apply learned ranks</h2>
<p><code>BpeTrainer::train_prepared</code> uses Chapter 2’s caller-supplied prepared-corpus reader. The
caller supplies the training-only stream, its expected SHA-256 and the identity
of the accepted corpus evidence. Training verifies the exact stream bytes and
rejects any supplied <code>split</code> metadata that is not <code>train</code>. These checks do not
discover overlap or establish rights, privacy or suitability; accepting that
preparation evidence remains the caller’s responsibility.</p>
<p>The existing trainer keeps its scalar learning path. The new method adds a
bounded working representation behind that same type; it does not define a
second tokenizer. The existing <code>BpeTokenizer</code> still owns token layout, frozen
rules, vocabulary expansions, document framing and byte decoding.</p>

<p>Each ingested byte becomes a token node with stable position, predecessor and
successor links. The input text is then released. Consumed nodes retain their
arena slots, so the node limit counts every ingested byte position. Node slots
and pair indexes stay in memory under caller-selected bounds. Streaming input
therefore does not mean constant-memory training or an external-memory algorithm.</p>
<p>A pair index records its current count and ordered live occurrence positions.
A priority queue puts the greatest count first, using the smallest numeric pair
when counts tie. Count updates can leave old queue entries behind. Each update
changes a generation number; a popped entry is usable only if its count and
generation still match the current pair state. A queue at its configured capacity
is rebuilt from current pairs, preserving the same winner order.</p>

<p>Replacing one pair removes the edge entering the left node, the selected edge,
and the edge leaving the right node, when those edges exist. The merged node
then supplies at most two new edges. Updating those edges immediately keeps
adjacent replacements from subtracting a shared old edge twice. Ordered live
positions enforce leftmost replacement; consumed overlapping occurrences vanish.</p>

<p>The scalar reference reuses the original trainer’s complete learning loop:
recount every current sequence, choose the winner and replace left to right.
<code>train_byte_fixture</code> supplies the same two byte documents to that loop. The
demo adapts its rules and counters into the artifact metadata used by the new
path; it does not write another learning loop. Both canonical payloads and
their hashes appear in the output, so their agreement can be inspected alongside
the different working representations.</p>

<p>Application has a different priority: the earliest learned rank among currently
adjacent eligible pairs, followed by the leftmost position. The encoder rechecks
adjacency and node versions before using a queued candidate, replaces that pair,
and queues its new neighbors. Rules are topological: a merge’s operands already
exist before that rule’s output ID is created.</p>

<p>Read chunks are transport boundaries, not token boundaries. <code>encode_reader_bounded</code>
reads one whole bounded document before encoding; callers invoke it separately
for each document. Literal text such as <code><|endoftext|></code> remains content bytes.
The existing document-framing operation inserts BOS and EOS after content
encoding. Byte decoding is exact; text decoding
checks UTF-8 after concatenating all token fragments, since an individual token
may contain only part of a UTF-8 character.</p>
<p><code>max_nodes</code> bounds all ingested training byte positions in one training call,
and byte positions in one encoded document. Bounded decoding uses that same
numeric limit as the maximum reconstructed content-byte count for one document;
it checks the total before allocating the output. A short token sequence can
still expand into too many bytes. The existing vocabulary constructor separately
bounds each token’s expansion with <code>max_token_bytes</code> and the sum of all content
expansions with <code>max_vocabulary_bytes</code>.</p>
<h3 id="preserve-the-artifact-and-its-evidence-boundary">Preserve the artifact and its evidence boundary</h3>
<p>The tokenizer artifact records its schema and layout, raw-byte policy, training
binding, requested merge count, ordered learned rules and efficiency counters.
Validation rejects unknown fields or versions, duplicate pairs, gaps, forward
operands and inconsistent reduction counts. Vocabulary expansions and output
serialization have explicit capacity checks.</p>

lineage. Producer timestamps, local paths and machine details belong in a separate
execution receipt. The two training strategies can emit equal tokenizer payload bytes
while having different producer receipts. Equal vocabulary size alone does not
identify the rules or their training source.</p>

<h2 id="history-subwords-still-need-a-boundary-policy">History: subwords still need a boundary policy</h2>
<p>A whole-word vocabulary leaves rare and unseen words difficult to represent;
learned subwords reduce that problem, but their alphabet and boundary rules still
determine which merges are possible.</p>
<p>In <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2016</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2016</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2016</span></span></span></span>, <a href="https://aclanthology.org/P16-1162/">Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units</a>
introduced BPE subword learning for neural translation. Sennrich and colleagues
learn subword units by repeatedly merging frequent symbol pairs, with word
boundaries retained in their character-based representation. That representation
is different from treating a complete document as one raw-byte sequence.</p>
<p>The published GPT-2 encoder applies a reversible byte-to-Unicode mapping, an
explicit pretokenization pattern and ranked merges within each resulting piece.
The pretokenization boundaries determine where a learned merge can apply.
Inspect <a href="https://github.com/openai/gpt-2/blob/e5c5054474f583d6d9499624649353995d63c70a/src/encoder.py">the pinned encoder implementation</a>.
The Unicode symbols represent bytes; the mapping does not normalize the input
text.</p>
<h3 id="isolate-one-letter-digit-boundary-in-rust">Isolate one letter-digit boundary in Rust</h3>
<p>Our chapter-local Rust example implements the published byte mapping and
pretokenization pattern. It reuses the course tokenizer’s existing frozen-rank
engine inside each piece, with one hypothetical merge of <code>a</code> followed by <code>1</code>.
This isolates boundary behavior without implementing BPE again. The demo’s
tiny vocabulary defines its displayed IDs; they are not the pretrained GPT-2
vocabulary’s IDs.</p>

<p>The raw-byte fixture learns <code>a1</code> from <code>a1a1</code> and encodes <code>a1</code> as one content
token. The published GPT-2 pattern splits <code>a1</code> into the letter piece <code>a</code> and
the digit piece <code>1</code> before BPE. The proposed merge cannot cross those pieces,
so this policy example emits two content tokens. Both paths reconstruct the
same input bytes. Reconstruction therefore does not imply equal segmentation.</p>

<p>The regex engine executes the fixed published pattern; Rust owns the byte map,
the existing rank decisions and the illustrative vocabulary IDs. The byte map
is reversible and does not create a merge across separate pieces. Here the
rank engine works on the pieces’ raw bytes; the resulting byte fragments are
then expressed through the map and tiny vocabulary. This demonstrates selected
published operations rather than reproducing the pretrained tokenizer.
Its bounded results do not establish agreement with every behavior of the
original Python regex runtime.</p>
<p>Freeze the training selection and tokenizer policy before constructing decoder
token targets. Improve the implementation without changing those learned
decisions or confusing byte reconstruction with equal segmentation.</p>

</ol>

<details><summary>Explanations for BPE counts, the third rank and pretoken boundaries</summary><ol>
<li>For <code>aaa</code>, the two adjacent <code>a,a</code> occurrences start at the first and second
positions. Replacing the first occurrence consumes the first two bytes, so the
overlapping occurrence cannot also be replaced. The result is one merged <code>aa</code>
token followed by the remaining <code>a</code> byte token.</li>
<li>After the two learned ranks for separate training documents <code>abab</code> and <code>abac</code>,
the current sequences are <code>[258,258]</code> and <code>[258,259]</code>, respectively. The
remaining pairs <code>(258,258)</code> and <code>(258,259)</code> each have count <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span> and left ID
<code>258</code>. Comparing right IDs selects <code>(258,258)</code> because <code>258</code> comes before
<code>259</code>. The new ID is <code>260</code>; <code>abab</code> becomes <code>[260]</code> and <code>abac</code> remains
<code>[258,259]</code>.</li>
<li>For input <code>a1</code>, byte reconstruction concatenates the token fragments.
The course raw-byte path applies its learned <code>a1</code> merge and emits one content
token. The GPT-2 pattern creates separate letter piece <code>a</code> and digit piece <code>1</code>
before BPE, so that merge cannot cross the pieces and the example emits two
content tokens. Both fragment sequences concatenate to the same <code>a1</code> bytes;
equal reconstruction does not imply equal segmentation.</li>
</ol></details>

<h2 id="hand-frozen-token-sequences-to-batching">Hand frozen token sequences to batching</h2>
<p>Use the frozen course tokenizer to encode each prepared document separately.
Held-out encoding does not fit new merges. Chapter 4 will place those token
sequences into variable-length batches without changing tokenizer identity.
The embedding and output layers must continue to interpret each content ID

commitmentMap.text:
# Current Practical Chapter 3 commitments

The current English candidate contains the home selector, practical index and
Practical Chapters 0–3. Chapter 0 explains the structure; later chapters teach
material. Current entries and navigation identify actual available chapters.
The first course ends at Chapter 39 and retains its implementation and accepted
wording. Practical lessons are English only, with localization support retained.
Applicable home, index, Chapter 0–2 and shared-surface commitments retain their
original concepts and evidence limits, interpreted against the current sources
and complete built pages.

The practical GPU path requires compatible NVIDIA hardware; CPU reference work,
prepared-corpus loading and the current tokenizer fixtures are usable on CPU.
External corpus preparation is replaceable and separate from the course-owned
Rust model. Bounded fixtures do not complete full preparation, accepted
full-corpus lineage, full tokenizer fitting, measured hardware or model quality.

## Existing implementation and decision rules

Chapter 3 extends the existing practical `BpeTrainer` and `BpeTokenizer`. The
original scalar learning loop supplies the recounting reference; existing
scalar ranked application supplies the application reference. Local pair
statistics and bounded live-adjacency application are strategies behind those
same owners. Layout, rules, operands, vocabulary expansion, framing and decoding
retain their existing owner. `train_byte_fixture` adapts input to the existing
learning loop. It does not copy that loop or define another tokenizer.

At each rank, count adjacent positions within each current training document,
including overlaps and excluding document boundaries and structural controls.
Select the greatest count; ties select the smallest left content ID and then
the smallest right content ID. Replace left to right without consuming an
input position twice. Consequently `aaa` has two counted occurrences and one
replacement; `aaaa` has three counted occurrences and two replacements.

The requested merge count is normally an upper limit. Prepared policy may
require an exact count and then refuses exhausted pairs. The trainer's count
and artifact policy must agree. Zero rounds is valid. The formula, its adjacent
selection explanation and definitions name the rank, pair IDs, integer count,
overlap/document scope and numeric tie order.

## Observed worked example

The separate training documents are `abab` and `abac`. BOS and EOS have IDs
`0,1`, one-byte content IDs are `2..257`, and `a,b,c` have IDs `99,100,101`.
There is no PAD. Before rank 0, counts are `(99,100):3`, `(99,101):1` and
`(100,99):2`. The selected `(99,100)` creates ID `258` with three replacements;
sequences become `[258,258]` and `[258,99,101]`.

Before rank 1, `(99,101)`, `(258,99)` and `(258,258)` each have count one.
Numeric order selects `(99,101)`, creating `259` with one replacement;
sequences become `[258,258]` and `[258,259]`. Held-out `acac` supplies no
learning counts. Frozen application emits `[259,259]`, reconstructs `acac`
and frames the document as `[0,259,259,1]`.

Both observed canonical payloads have SHA-256
`8b1534b8711b1b55c97466fcdd94c6059395acf553e25ba66a6e4911604014b9`.
Eight training input bytes produce four content tokens. Four inserted controls
for two documents are excluded from the numerator: 0.5 content tokens per
input byte. Empty input has no defined ratio. Eighteen local edge updates,
eight peak node slots, four peak pair types, eleven peak heap entries and zero
rebuilds are logical working-representation observations, not measured RAM or
throughput. Sequence length, memory, speed and model quality remain distinct.

## Local updates, application and bounds

Stable nodes retain predecessor/successor links. A replacement removes the
existing incoming, selected and outgoing edges, then immediately adds new
neighbor edges. Ordered occurrences preserve leftmost nonoverlapping
replacement. Queue order preserves maximum count/minimum pair; generations
reject stale entries, and a capacity rebuild uses current pair states.

Consumed slots remain allocated. `max_nodes` counts all ingested byte positions;
documents, pair types, heap entries and trace values have distinct limits.
Weighted fixture records use checked counts without allocating every repeated
copy. Streaming input releases document text but retains the bounded working
representation. This is neither constant-memory nor external-memory training.
Avoiding unaffected-edge recounts establishes no measured speed improvement.

Frozen application selects the earliest eligible learned rank, then the
leftmost position, and rechecks adjacency and versions. Operands must precede
their rule's output. Reader chunks are transport boundaries: one bounded whole
document is collected, and separate documents require separate calls.
Decoding concatenates existing byte expansions exactly; text decoding checks
UTF-8 after concatenation. Literal control spellings are ordinary content.
The existing framing validator owns BOS/EOS placement. Decoded output size is
checked before allocation; per-token and total-vocabulary expansion limits
separately bound expansion work.

## Corpus and artifact evidence

The caller supplies a training-only prepared stream and accepts its corpus
evidence. The existing reader decodes documents; training verifies exact source
SHA-256 and refuses supplied non-training split metadata. These checks do not
discover overlap or certify rights, privacy, quality or suitability.

The artifact records closed schema/layout, raw-byte policy, training binding,
requested count, ordered rules and counters. Course-owned checks reject unknown
fields/versions, duplicate pairs, rank gaps, forward operands and inconsistent
reductions; existing tokenizer construction validates vocabulary expansions.
JSON syntax is supporting plumbing. Fixed canonical payload bytes identify
rules and declared lineage. Producer timestamps, paths and machines belong in
separate receipts. Equal vocabulary size does not identify a tokenizer.

## History, comparison and reproduction

Sennrich and colleagues' 2016 subword method repeatedly merges frequent symbol
pairs in a character representation retaining word boundaries. The pinned
published GPT-2 encoder applies a reversible byte map, its concrete
pretokenization pattern and frozen ranks within each piece. The boundaries
determine where a learned merge can apply.

The chapter-local Rust example implements that byte mapping and fixed pattern,
reuses the existing course rank engine and supplies a tiny illustrative
vocabulary. Its IDs are not pretrained GPT-2 IDs. For `a1`, the course raw-byte
path uses a merge learned from `a1a1` and emits `[258]` with fragment `6131`.
The separate pattern example emits pieces `a,1`, illustrative IDs `[64,16]`
and fragments `61,31`. Both reconstruct `a1`; reconstruction does not imply
equal segmentation. The supporting regex engine performs pattern matching,
not course BPE, byte-map, pattern-choice, rank or vocabulary decisions.
This is no full-pretrained-tokenizer or Python-runtime parity claim.

No foreign tokenizer supplies an assertion, oracle, snapshot, parity or
admission gate. Historical outputs are displayed observations. Own-course
tests compare scalar and extended strategies: every rank for 100 seeded
three-document corpora, lengths 0–32 over `a..h`, and application/decoding for
10,000 strings of length 0–64 mixing `a..c` and arbitrary bytes. They reuse
SplitMix64 with seed `0x42b0d5eed`. Sixteen integration and three demo tests
passed, including the optional third-rank exercise. Current formatted workspace
validation passed 501 tests, Clippy and format checks.

Learner run instructions supply repository-root context, Docker/workspace
prerequisites, copyable commands and observable output. The nonquiet Cargo demo
and both exact single-test selectors executed successfully in the cached
offline image; each selector ran exactly one test. Wrapper provisioning was
not run under the offline execution boundary. Practice and answers explain
overlap, the next own-course tie and pretoken boundaries.

Freeze tokenizer policy before decoder targets and encode each document with
the same frozen vocabulary. The Chapter 4 batching handoff describes later
material, not an already available chapter or measured capability.

# Current practical foundation commitments

These author-owned commitments describe the meaning carried by the scoped
English home, practical index and Practical Chapters 0–2. They are checked
against the bound current source, built HTML and technical evidence. They
supply no candidate classification or judgment verdict. Each actual review
surface carries its separately frozen neutral role requirement.

## Home, index and course boundaries

- The home offers two named courses and two named start actions. LLM from
  scratch builds a small Rust language model through Chapters 0–39. Practical
  LLM in Rust extends a separate founding copy of that completed model.
- Chapter 0 explains the practical course's structure. Chapter 1 and later
  chapters contain learning material. The practical index links to the available
  lessons and distinguishes them from the later roadmap.
- The practical course requires the first course's basics or equivalent Rust
