def create_ids_to_remove_files(ids_to_remove_dir: Path, num_files: int = 5) -> list[int]:
    """Create parquet files containing IDs to remove (random ints 0-999, split into num_files)."""
    ids_to_remove_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    ids = list(range(0, 1000, 5))
    random.shuffle(ids)
    chunks = np.array_split(ids, num_files)
    for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
        pd.DataFrame({"id": chunk}).to_parquet(ids_to_remove_dir / f"ids_to_remove_{i}.parquet", index=False)
    return ids


def create_input_files(input_dir: Path, num_files: int = 100) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, list[str]]:
    """Create input parquet files, each with 10 rows: 0-9, 10-19, ..., up to num_files*10-1."""
    input_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    id_chunks = np.array_split(np.arange(num_files * 10), num_files)
    all_data = []
    for i, ids in enumerate(id_chunks):
        df = pd.DataFrame(
            {
                CURATOR_DEDUP_ID_STR: ids,
                "text": [f"Document {i}" for i in ids],
                "category": [f"category_{j % 10}" for j in ids],
                "score": [0.9 + (j % 10) * 0.01 for j in ids],
            }
        )
        df.to_parquet(input_dir / f"input_file_{i}.parquet", index=False)
        all_data.append(df)
    return pd.concat(all_data, ignore_index=True), [
        str(input_dir / f"input_file_{i}.parquet") for i in range(num_files)
    ]


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "test_config",
    [
        pytest.param((RayDataExecutor, {}), id="ray_data"),
        pytest.param((XennaExecutor, {"execution_mode": "streaming"}), id="xenna"),
    ],
    indirect=True,
)
class TestTextDuplicateRemovalWorkflowIntegration:
    """Integration tests for TextDuplicatesRemovalWorkflow with different executors."""

    # Class attributes for shared test data
    executor_cls: type | None = None
    config: dict[str, Any] | None = None
    input_dir: Path | None = None
    ids_to_remove_dir: Path | None = None
    output_dir: Path | None = None
    expected_input_df: pd.DataFrame | None = None
    ids_to_remove: list[int] | None = None
    workflow_output: WorkflowRunResult | None = None
    output_tasks: list[DocumentBatch] | None = None

    @pytest.fixture
    def test_config(
        self, request: pytest.FixtureRequest, tmp_path_factory: pytest.TempPathFactory
    ) -> "TestTextDuplicateRemovalWorkflowIntegration":
        """Set up test environment and execute the duplicate removal workflow."""
        executor_cls, config = request.param

        self.executor_cls = executor_cls
        self.config = config

        # Create temporary directories
        tmp_path = tmp_path_factory.mktemp("removal_workflow_integration")
        self.input_dir = tmp_path / "input"
        self.ids_to_remove_dir = tmp_path / "ids_to_remove"
        self.output_dir = tmp_path / "output"

        # Create test data
        self.expected_input_df, self.input_file_paths = create_input_files(self.input_dir, num_files=100)
        self.ids_to_remove = create_ids_to_remove_files(self.ids_to_remove_dir, num_files=5)

        # Create and run workflow
        workflow = TextDuplicatesRemovalWorkflow(
            input_path=str(self.input_dir),
            ids_to_remove_path=str(self.ids_to_remove_dir),
            output_path=str(self.output_dir),
            input_filetype="parquet",
            output_filetype="parquet",
            id_field=CURATOR_DEDUP_ID_STR,
            duplicate_id_field="id",
            input_kwargs={},
            duplicate_id_read_kwargs={},
            output_kwargs={},
        )

        executor = executor_cls(config)
        workflow_output = workflow.run(executor)
        self.workflow_output = workflow_output
        # Extract tasks from the "removal" pipeline
        self.output_tasks = workflow_output.pipeline_tasks.get("removal", [])

        return self

    def test_output_correctness_and_files(self, test_config: "TestTextDuplicateRemovalWorkflowIntegration"):
        """Test output correctness and file system integrity."""
        assert test_config.workflow_output is not None
        assert test_config.workflow_output.pipeline_tasks
        assert test_config.workflow_output.get_metadata("total_time") > 0
        assert test_config.output_tasks is not None
        assert test_config.expected_input_df is not None
        assert test_config.ids_to_remove is not None
        assert test_config.output_dir is not None
        assert test_config.output_dir.exists()

        # Verify output files exist and are readable
        all_output_files = []
        for task in test_config.output_tasks:
            all_output_files.extend(task.data)
        assert len(all_output_files) > 0

        # Combine all output data for comprehensive correctness check
        combined_output_df = pd.concat(
            [pd.read_parquet(task.data) for task in test_config.output_tasks], ignore_index=True
        )

        # Expected: all IDs from input that are NOT in ids_to_remove
        expected_ids = set(test_config.expected_input_df[CURATOR_DEDUP_ID_STR].tolist()) - set(
            test_config.ids_to_remove
        )
        actual_ids = set(combined_output_df[CURATOR_DEDUP_ID_STR].tolist())

        # Core correctness checks
        assert actual_ids == expected_ids
        assert len(combined_output_df) == 800  # 1000 total input - 200 divisible by 5

        # Verify no IDs divisible by 5 remain
        remaining_divisible_by_5 = [id_val for id_val in actual_ids if id_val % 5 == 0]
        assert len(remaining_divisible_by_5) == 0, f"Found IDs divisible by 5: {remaining_divisible_by_5}"

        # Verify expected columns are present
        expected_columns = {"text", "category", "score", CURATOR_DEDUP_ID_STR}
        assert set(combined_output_df.columns) == expected_columns

        # Verify individual files are valid parquet files with correct data
        total_records = 0
        for file_path in all_output_files:
            assert file_path.endswith(".parquet"), f"Expected parquet file, got {file_path}"
            df = pd.read_parquet(file_path)
            total_records += len(df)

            # Each file should have expected columns
            assert set(df.columns) == expected_columns

            # No IDs divisible by 5 in any individual file
            ids_in_file = df[CURATOR_DEDUP_ID_STR].tolist()
            divisible_by_5 = [id_val for id_val in ids_in_file if id_val % 5 == 0]
            assert len(divisible_by_5) == 0, f"File {file_path} contains IDs divisible by 5: {divisible_by_5}"

        # Total records across all files should match combined total
        assert total_records == 800

        # Metadata summaries should agree with observed behavior
        assert test_config.workflow_output.get_metadata("num_duplicates_removed") == 200

    def test_metadata_num_removed_consistency(self, test_config: "TestTextDuplicateRemovalWorkflowIntegration"):
        """Test that num_removed metadata sums up correctly across all tasks."""
        assert test_config.output_tasks is not None
        assert test_config.ids_to_remove is not None

        # Sum up all num_removed from task metadata
        total_removed_from_metadata = sum(task._metadata["num_removed"] for task in test_config.output_tasks)

        # Expected total removed based on actual workflow behavior
        # The workflow removes 2 records per input file (from 10 records to 8 records)
        # With 100 input files, total removed should be 200
        expected_total_removed = 200  # 2 * 100 files

        assert total_removed_from_metadata == expected_total_removed
        assert test_config.workflow_output is not None
        assert test_config.workflow_output.get_metadata("num_duplicates_removed") == expected_total_removed

        # Also verify by checking the actual difference in record counts
        total_input_records = len(test_config.expected_input_df)
        total_output_records = 0
        for task in test_config.output_tasks:
            for file_path in task.data:
                df = pd.read_parquet(file_path)
                total_output_records += len(df)

        actual_records_removed = total_input_records - total_output_records
        assert actual_records_removed == expected_total_removed

    def test_initial_tasks_partitioning(self, test_config: "TestTextDuplicateRemovalWorkflowIntegration"):
        """Test workflow with initial_tasks - should create 20 output tasks from 100 input files grouped 5 at a time."""
        assert test_config.input_file_paths is not None

        assert isinstance(stages[1], expected_reader_stage)

    "# End-to-end fuzzy deduplication\n",
    "\n",
    "GPU accelerated implementation of a MinHash-LSH based fuzzy deduplication. For more information about fuzzy deduplication in NeMo Curator, refer to the [Deduplication](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/curator/latest/curate-text/process-data/deduplication/index.html) section of the documentation page.\n",
    "\n",
    "The tutorial here shows how to run fuzzy deduplication on text data by executing 2 end to end workflows.\n",
    "These 2 workflows roughly cover the following steps to perform fuzzy deduplication:\n",
    "\n",
    "1. Read original dataset\n",
    "2. Compute MinHashes signatures of these documents\n",
    "3. Perform LSH - Group Minhashes into bands/buckets and shuffle these bands/buckets so that documents in the same bucket are in the same batch/file.\n",
    "4. Convert the LSH outputs (bucket_id -> doc_id mapping) into an edgelist in preparation for connected components. \n",
    "5. Compute connected components across all potential duplicates found via LSH.\n",
    "6. Generate list of duplicate documents by randomly selecting 1 document to keep from each group/component and dropping the rest.\n",
    "7. Remove duplicates based on the generated duplicate list.\n",
    "\n",
    "We also allow users to also run these steps independently, which will be covered in the step by step tutorial in the same directory as this tutorial."
   ]

    "## Running as a Single Stage (End-to-End)\n",
    "\n",
    "See the [API Reference](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/curator/latest/apidocs/stages/stages.deduplication.fuzzy.workflow.html#api) for more information about the `FuzzyDeduplicationWorkflow` class.\n",
    "\n",
    "### General Notes\n",
    "#### ID Generation\n",
    "1. The ID generation process requires a Ray cluster to be started before running the workflow either from the CLI or by using the `RayClient` API in Curator.\n",
    "2. The `FuzzyDeduplicationWorkflow` API doesn't utilize any existing IDs in the input dataset and instead generates IDs on the fly using an ID Generator actor.\n",
    "3. The ID Generator gives each row a unique increasing integer ID, based on the order files are read.\n",
    "4. This avoids expensive ID->Integer encoding for the underlying connected components algorithm which only supports integer IDs.\n",
    "5. When we find duplicates, we save these integer IDs in sorted files with multiple row groups.\n",
    "6. We also save a `fuzzy_id_generator.json` which maintains a mapping of input file partitions to ID ranges for that batch.\n",
    "7. During removal, reading the same file groups will give the same integer IDs, using the min/max ID values, we can find all corresponding duplicates in that range making the process faster.\n",
    "\n",
    "#### Performance Considerations\n",
    "1. LSH - Configuring `bands_per_iteration` controls how many bands to process simultaneously in a single shuffle. Higher values can lead to faster performance but might increase memory pressure.\n",
    "2. A low `input_blocksize` may not saturate the GPUs enough while a high `input_blocksize` can lead to OOM errors during MinHash and excessive object store usage during removal. It's recommend to keep it at 512MiB-1.5GiB and reduce if running into OOMs during MinHash.\n",
    "3. The removal step can be memory intensive and it's recommend to set a higher fraction of object store memory for removal (if the machine has enough RAM). The `RayDataExecutor` showed better results during duplicate removal.\n",
    "4. The removal workflow is CPU only and can be run  on machines that don't have GPUs\n",
    "\n",
    "#### Hyperparameter Considerations\n",
    "1. The current defaults for fuzzy deduplication (260 hashes, 13 hashes per band) approximate finding documents with a Jaccard similarity of 0.8. For more information on selecting the number of bands/hashes it's recommended to analyze the S curve and tolerable threshold for false positives (and negatives). More information about LSH can be found in section `3.4.2` [here](http://infolab.stanford.edu/~ullman/mmds/ch3n.pdf).\n",
    "2. The `char_ngrams` values of 24 is set to approximate roughly ngrams that correspond to ~5 words.\n"

    "#### Advanced: Looking at examples of duplicate documents\n",
    "\n",
    "1. This analysis involves re-reading the input data with the same ID mapping that was used during duplicate identification.\n",
    "2. Merging the input data with the connected components results on the `_curator_dedup_id` column to associate each document which the duplicate group it belongs to which can be used for further analysis.\n",
    "\n",
    "**NOTE**: This analysis approach is intended as an example for smaller datasets and only works for cases where the connected components dataframe is small and fits comfortable in memory. It is not recommended for larger datasets."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",

   "id": "7ef243e5-b8df-47d5-b993-fa61a3954eee",

   "source": [
    "from nemo_curator.pipeline import Pipeline\n",
    "from nemo_curator.stages.base import ProcessingStage\n",
    "from nemo_curator.stages.resources import Resources\n",
    "from nemo_curator.stages.text.io.reader import JsonlReader, ParquetReader\n",
    "from nemo_curator.tasks.document import DocumentBatch\n",
    "\n",
    "\n",
    "class CustomMergeStage(ProcessingStage[DocumentBatch, DocumentBatch]):\n",
    "    \"\"\"\n",
    "    Warning: This should not be attempted with large connected components results.\n",
    "    A small stage that merges the input data (using the id's generated) with the connected components result.\n",
    "    Works because CC results are small enough to fit per batch.\n",
    "    \"\"\"\n",
    "\n",
    "    resources = Resources(cpus=1.0)\n",
    "\n",
    "    def process(self, batch: DocumentBatch) -> DocumentBatch:\n",
    "        df = batch.to_pandas().merge(cc_df, how=\"inner\", on=[CURATOR_DEDUP_ID_STR])\n",
    "        return DocumentBatch(\n",
    "            dataset_name=batch.dataset_name, data=df, _stage_perf=batch._stage_perf\n",
    "        )\n",
    "\n",
    "\n",
    "ReaderClass = ParquetReader if input_filetype == \"parquet\" else JsonlReader\n",
    "pipeline = Pipeline(\n",
    "    name=\"Explore duplicates\",\n",
    "    stages=[\n",
    "        ReaderClass(file_paths=input_dataset_path, blocksize=input_blocksize, _assign_ids=True, read_kwargs=io_kwargs),\n",
    "        CustomMergeStage(),\n",
    "    ],\n",
    ")"
   ]
  },

      "author_observation": {
        "source_id": "SRC-DTH-TOK-04",
        "paraphrase": "The published GPT-2 encoder builds a reversible representation of all 256 byte values as Unicode symbols. Its pretokenization expression separates categories such as letters and numbers before BPE. Within each resulting piece, the encoder chooses the adjacent pair with the smallest learned rank, merges nonoverlapping occurrences and repeats. Encoding converts each piece to UTF-8 bytes before mapping those bytes; decoding joins the token symbols, maps them back to bytes and then decodes the combined byte sequence. Chapter 42 reproduces these operations with a tiny illustrative vocabulary to expose the letter-versus-digit boundary in `a1`. That vocabulary is course-authored and supplies no pretrained GPT-2 token IDs or tokenizer parity result.",

    "source_id": "SRC-DTH-TOK-04",
    "paraphrase": "The published GPT-2 encoder builds a reversible representation of all 256 byte values as Unicode symbols. Its pretokenization expression separates categories such as letters and numbers before BPE. Within each resulting piece, the encoder chooses the adjacent pair with the smallest learned rank, merges nonoverlapping occurrences and repeats. Decontamination Check and exclude training overlap with declared protected evaluation material using a specified method. Passing that check does not establish absence of every possible leak. Document occurrence One stored instance of a document. Two records containing the same text are two occurrences and can give that text extra training weight. Exact deduplication Remove repeated text under a declared equality policy. The NeMo example groups text hashes and keeps one representative; it does not detect paraphrases or certify collision-proof equality. Held-out split Validation or test documents kept out of tokenizer learning and model fitting. Validation informs setting choices; test evaluation is reserved for the final assessment. Near-duplicate A document sufficiently similar to another under a declared matching method. Approximate searches can miss related text or group text that should remain distinct. Prepared-document interchange UTF-8 JSONL records with nonblank string id and text fields and retained metadata. Rust loads the supplied selection without redoing filtering, duplicate removal or split assignment. Retention fraction Prepared-document count divided by input-document count for a nonempty input. It measures how much the declared pipeline retains, not the quality of its survivors. Source group Records declared to belong to one related source family. The exercise assigns each supplied group to a single split; that assignment does not prove all related records were discovered. BPE merge A learned rule that joins two adjacent content tokens. Training selects by current frequency; overlapping occurrences count, but replacements proceed left to right without overlap. Byte coverage An initial content token for every possible byte value, so any byte sequence has a fallback encoding. Byte coverage does not imply that each token fragment is valid UTF-8. Merge rank A rule's position in the learned order. Encoding prioritizes the earliest learned eligible rule, then the leftmost live occurrence. Pretokenization Splitting input into pieces before BPE. Merges stay inside a piece; the chapter's GPT-2 policy example separates a letter from a digit, while the course policy has no internal pretoken boundaries. Special token A structural control inserted through an explicit API. The course tokenizer reserves BOS and EOS; ordinary text, including control-looking spellings, cannot insert those IDs. Tokenizer identity The exact learned payload and its declared training lineage, including layout, policy and ordered merges. Equal vocabulary sizes or reconstructed text do not identify the same tokenizer. Tokens per byte Content-token count divided by input-byte count for nonempty content. isolated.value: For aaa, the two adjacent a,a occurrences start at the first and second positions. Replacing the first occurrence consumes the first two bytes, so the overlapping occurrence cannot also be replaced. The result is one merged aa token followed by the remaining a byte token. After the two learned ranks for separate training documents abab and abac, the current sequences are [258,258] and [258,259], respectively. The remaining pairs (258,258) and (258,259) each have count 1 and left ID 258. Comparing right IDs selects (258,258) because 258 comes before 259. The new ID is 260; abab becomes [260] and abac remains [258,259]. For input a1, byte reconstruction concatenates the token fragments. The course raw-byte path applies its learned a1 merge and emits one content token. The GPT-2 pattern creates separate letter piece a and digit piece 1 before BPE, so that merge cannot cross the pieces and the example emits two content tokens. Both fragment sequences concatenate to the same a1 bytes; equal reconstruction does not imply equal segmentation.

isolated.value: Visit leftmost live matches, remove disappearing edges once and add the new neighboring edges after each replacement. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/tokenizer/incremental.rs#local-edge-replacement fn replace(&mut self, pair: TokenPair, output: u32) -> Result<u64, TokenizerError> { let mut replacements = 0u64; // Stable indices follow source order; first() gives the leftmost live match. while let Some(left) = self .pairs .get(&pair) .and_then(|s| s.occurrences.first()) .copied() { if self.edge(left) != Some(pair) { return Err(TokenizerError::Invariant("stale live occurrence")); } let right = self.nodes[left] .next .ok_or(TokenizerError::Invariant("pair has no right node"))?; let previous = self.nodes[left].previous; let next = self.nodes[right].next; // Three distinct edge starts disappear; adjacent replacements cannot // remove a shared old edge twice because the lists update immediately. if let Some(index) = previous { self.remove_edge(index)?; } self.remove_edge(left)?; self.remove_edge(right)?; self.nodes[left].token = output; self.nodes[left].next = next; self.nodes[right].alive = false; if let Some(index) = next { self.nodes[index].previous = Some(left); } if let Some(index) = previous { self.add_edge(index)?; } self.add_edge(left)?; replacements = replacements .checked_add(self.weights[self.nodes[left].document]) .ok_or(TokenizerError::Overflow)?; } Ok(replacements) }

isolated.value: Adapt the existing scalar trainer's learned rules and counters to the same artifact fields, without using the local pair index. rust/demos/practical-ch03-scalable-bpe-tokenizer/src/lib.rs#scalar-rank-reference fn scalar_fixture( template: &artifact::TokenizerArtifact, documents: &[PreparedDocument], ) -> Result<artifact::TokenizerArtifact, String> { let bytes = documents .iter() .map(|document| document.text.as_bytes().to_vec()) .collect::<Vec<_>>(); let learned = BpeTrainer::new(template.policy.merge_count) .train_byte_fixture(&bytes) .map_err(|error| error.to_string())?; let tokenizer = BpeTokenizer::from_training(&learned).map_err(|error| error.to_string())?; let merges = learned .rules() .iter() .zip(tokenizer.merge_rules()) .map(|(learned, frozen)| { Ok(artifact::ArtifactMerge { candidate_count: u64::try_from(learned.candidate_count()) .map_err(|error| error.to_string())?, left: frozen.content_pair().left(), rank: frozen.rank(), replacements: u64::try_from(learned.replacement_count()) .map_err(|error| error.to_string())?, right: frozen.content_pair().right(), token_id: frozen.content_token_id(), }) }) .collect::<Result<Vec<_>, String>>()?; let count = |lengths: Vec<usize>| -> Result<u64, String> { lengths.into_iter().try_fold(0u64, |total, length| { total .checked_add(u64::try_from(length).map_err(|error| error.to_string())?) .ok_or_else(|| "scalar fixture count overflow".to_owned()) }) }; let training_documents = u64::try_from(documents.len()).map_err(|error| error.to_string())?; let mut result = template.clone(); result.merges = merges; result.counters = artifact::EfficiencyCounters { content_tokens: count(learned.final_sequences().iter().map(Vec::len).collect())?, control_tokens: training_documents .checked_mul(2) .ok_or("scalar fixture control count overflow")?, input_bytes: count(bytes.iter().map(Vec::len).collect())?, training_documents, }; Ok(result) }

|| self.counters.content_tokens > self.counters.input_bytes { return Err(TokenizerError::Artifact("inconsistent efficiency counters")); } let layout = TokenizerLayout::new(self.merges.len())?; let mut pairs = Vec::new(); pairs .try_reserve_exact(self.merges.len()) .map_err(|_| TokenizerError::Resource("merge operand allocation failed"))?; let mut reduction = 0u64; for (rank, rule) in self.merges.iter().enumerate() { if rule.rank != rank || layout.merge_token_id(rank) != Some(rule.token_id) || rule.replacements == 0 || rule.replacements > rule.candidate_count { return Err(TokenizerError::Artifact("invalid rank or merge count")); } let left = rule .left .checked_sub(CONTENT_ID_OFFSET) .ok_or(TokenizerError::Artifact( "control ID cannot be a merge operand", ))?; let right = rule.right .checked_sub(CONTENT_ID_OFFSET) .ok_or(TokenizerError::Artifact( "control ID cannot be a merge operand", ))?; pairs.push(TokenPair::new(left, right)); reduction = reduction .checked_add(rule.replacements) .ok_or(TokenizerError::Overflow)?; } if self.counters.input_bytes.checked_sub(reduction) != Some(self.counters.content_tokens) { return Err(TokenizerError::Artifact( "merge reductions disagree with content count", )); } // This single constructor owns prior-rank operands, duplicate pairs, // byte expansions and their bounds; there is no second vocabulary here. Ok(BpeTokenizer::from_merge_pairs_bounded( &pairs, limits.max_token_bytes, limits.max_vocabulary_bytes, )?) }

isolated.value: Map each possible byte to a reversible Unicode symbol and define the chapter's illustrative vocabulary IDs. rust/demos/practical-ch03-scalable-bpe-tokenizer/src/gpt2_contrast.rs#gpt2-byte-mapping let mut byte_order = (b'!'..=b'~') .chain(0xa1..=0xac) .chain(0xae..=0xff) .collect::<Vec<_>>(); let mut symbols = byte_order .iter() .map(|&byte| char::from(byte)) .collect::<Vec<_>>(); let mut next_codepoint = 256u32; for byte in 0..=255u8 { if !byte_order.contains(&byte) { let symbol = char::from_u32(next_codepoint).ok_or("invalid byte-map symbol")?; byte_order.push(byte); symbols.push(symbol); next_codepoint += 1; } } let mut bytes = ['\0'; 256]; let mut reverse_bytes = BTreeMap::new(); let mut vocabulary = BTreeMap::new(); for (id, (&byte, &symbol)) in byte_order.iter().zip(&symbols).enumerate() { bytes[byte as usize] = symbol; reverse_bytes.insert(symbol, byte); vocabulary.insert(symbol.to_string(), id as u32); }

Follow the practical path
Chapter 1: Record the reference model binds the tiny experiment to its inputs and separates repeatable results from claims about language quality or speed. Chapter 2: Prepare a corpus separates external text preparation from Rust loading, and preserves document and split identity. Chapter 3 extends byte-pair encoding. It adds bounded ingestion, local pair updates and efficient application of frozen merge ranks to the existing tokenizer.
The practical course index links to the lessons currently available. The later curriculum continues with variable-length batches and packing, configurable decoder depth and shape, GPU execution, larger training runs, complete resume state, evaluation, adaptation, quantized inference and serving. These are stages of one causal text model. Their examples become available as each mechanism is implemented and measured.

Keep the completed model as the starting point
The first course builds the mechanisms of a small causal language model. This course begins with its completed implementation and studies how data handling, execution, training and inference must change for larger workloads. The Rust implementation for this course lives in rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical. Its examples extend that copy; the first course keeps its own implementation.

Read the examples at their stated scale
Small fixtures make intermediate values inspectable: a pair count, a token sequence, a loss or a restored state. They establish the behavior shown for those inputs. They do not establish full-corpus throughput, useful generated language, or a larger model’s memory use. Full-data runs and hardware measurements supply that separate evidence.

Start from a working model
This course starts from a working language model and studies what must change as the data, model and workload grow. The starting implementation is a separate copy of the model completed in LLM from scratch. It already contains byte-pair tokenization, tensors, automatic differentiation, a causal decoder, training, evaluation, checkpoints and cached generation. Here we extend those parts.
Chapter 0 is an orientation. Chapter 1 begins the learning material by recording exactly what the small reference model demonstrates. That record gives later changes a concrete comparison point.

History: reporting conditions and measuring variation
A language-model score without its input conditions and scope does not identify what was evaluated or establish which capabilities were checked.
Model Cards for Model Reporting was presented in 2019. Mitchell and colleagues propose model documentation that includes intended uses and evaluation conditions; a model card is not itself proof of quality.
Model Cards describe evaluation conditions and intended uses; later fine-tuning experiments study variation across initializations and data orders. Reporting scope and measuring variation answer different questions.
In Fine-Tuning Pretrained Language Models: Weight Initializations, Data Orders, and Early Stopping, published in 2020, Dodge and colleagues study fine-tuning variability associated with initialization and data order for pretrained language models. This does not measure variability in the course’s tiny decoder.
Keep a fixed regression reference when changing an LLM pipeline, while recording separately the evidence needed for quality, seed sensitivity and hardware claims.

trace .observation() .final_evaluation() .decoder() .mean_nll()

reading.value:
The problem: changes need a fixed comparison point
The final chapter of LLM from scratch joined the tokenizer, decoder, training, evaluation, checkpoint and generation code. This practical course starts from a separate copy of that implementation. If the data, configuration and code change together, a changed result no longer tells you which version you observed. You need a fixed reference that identifies its inputs and states exactly what its checks establish.
This chapter runs the completed first-course pipeline without modifying it. The practical copy can then evolve while this comparison point stays fixed. The example gives that reference an input identity and a report whose claims stay attached to their evidence. The identity identifies the fixed inputs. The checks establish which behavior this execution reproduced. Neither establishes useful laptop-scale capability.
What the reference actually does
The fixture assigns 8 documents to training, 2 to validation and 2 to test. The decoder has 1188 learned scalar parameters and context capacity 4 tokens. Its primary training schedule and separately executed replay each perform 32 updates on full batches of 16 windows, with 4 valid targets per window. Therefore, each schedule consumes
32\cdot16\cdot4=2048

valid training targets. One pipeline invocation includes both schedules: 4096 targets altogether. These counts are derived from the frozen full-batch schedule, not from a new runtime token counter. Evaluation targets and generated tokens are separate quantities.
The report’s independent_schedules field counts two separately executed copies of the same schedule from training seed 39, not statistically independent seed samples.
The replay agrees bit for bit with the primary training result in this execution. The selected decoder and frozen bigram then score the same 1744 overlapping test-window target slots. Their mean negative log-likelihoods are approximately 3.866087547 and 3.981342714 nats per slot, respectively. This known comparison is a regression check: rerunning it can expose changes in the checked behavior. It is not an independent estimate of generalization.
There are only 442 within-document transition occurrences in those test documents. Overlapping windows repeat occurrences, so 1744 is not a count of distinct transitions. A separate policy would score each occurrence once, using the longest available causal prefix capped at four tokens and only its newest-position distribution. This run does not report numeric mean NLL or perplexity under that policy.
The checkpoint round trip preserves its encoded bytes, model and optimizer bits, and tokenizer. The restored decoder reproduces logits for the fixed At probe, encoded as token IDs [67,118]. Cached and complete-prefix generation agree on token IDs [260,34,34]: Cyrillic т followed by two spaces. Agreement checks the two generation paths; those three tokens do not demonstrate useful language quality.

The solution: identify inputs, then interpret evidence
R_{\mathrm{ref}}=\operatorname{SHA256}(\mathrm{config}_{1188}\Vert\mathrm{fixture}\Vert\mathrm{source\_revision})

The identity’s symbols and fixed settings
R_{\mathrm{ref}} is a 256-bit digest, displayed as 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters. Its three named inputs are:
\mathrm{config}_{1188}: a canonical record of eighteen tiny-run settings, together with the invariant that the decoder has 1188 parameters. \mathrm{fixture}: a canonical record of SHA-256 digests of the exact corpus bytes and exact split-manifest bytes. Even a byte change that leaves parsed JSON meaning unchanged creates a different input identity. \mathrm{source\_revision}: a verified source identity combining a baseline revision with the exact forty Rust source files of the completed first-course crate, including its module declarations in lib.rs.
Here \Vert means composition into the shared identity format’s named, canonical fields, not writing three unframed strings beside one another. That distinction matters: without field boundaries, different input sequences can have the same concatenated bytes. The helper orders fields, serializes one unambiguous record and hashes its complete bytes.
The settings fix eight BPE merges; decoder width, feed-forward width and context capacity of four; one attention head and one block; stride one; training and evaluation batch sizes of sixteen and one hundred twenty-eight; thirty-two updates; learning rate 0.04; gradient-norm cap 1; training seed 39; generation seed 38; bigram smoothing 1; generation temperature 0.8; top-k four; and three generated tokens. The identity records floating-point settings by their exact bit patterns rather than rounded display text.

Reject changed fixtures, run the unchanged scalar pipeline and retain only its checked observation. rust/demos/practical-ch01-reference-core-handoff/src/lib.rs#reference-handoff /// Refuse changed fixtures before model/checkpoint work, then call the existing /// capstone once. That call already includes primary training and full replay. pub fn run_reference_handoff( corpus_source: &str, split_source: &str, checkpoint_path: impl AsRef<Path>, source: &ReferenceSourceProof, ) -> Result<ReferenceHandoffTrace, ReferenceHandoffError> { if sha256(corpus_source.as_bytes()).as_hex() != CORPUS_SHA256 { return Err(ReferenceHandoffError::FixtureMismatch("corpus")); } if sha256(split_source.as_bytes()).as_hex() != SPLITS_SHA256 { return Err(ReferenceHandoffError::FixtureMismatch("split manifest")); } // Safe callers obtain this opaque proof only through the foundation's // approved-manifest/compiled-census verification, not a revision string. let identity = reference_input_identity( &tiny_config_identity()?, corpus_source.as_bytes(), split_source.as_bytes(), source.identity(), )?; let digest = identity.digest()?; let observation = run_capstone( corpus_source, split_source, checkpoint_path, CapstoneConfig::tiny(), )?; let evaluation = observation.final_evaluation(); let checkpoint = observation.checkpoint(); if observation.training().parameter_count() != 1188 || observation.training().optimizer_step() != 32 || !observation.training().replay_bitwise() || evaluation.window_count() != 436 || evaluation.window_target_slot_count() != 1744 || evaluation.document_transition_occurrence_count() != 442 || !evaluation.decoder().mean_nll().is_finite() || !evaluation.bigram().mean_nll().is_finite() || !checkpoint.bytes_roundtrip() || !checkpoint.model_bits_exact() || !checkpoint.optimizer_bits_exact() || !checkpoint.tokenizer_exact() || !checkpoint.prompt_logits_bitwise() || !observation.generation().tokens_exact() || !observation.generation().decisions_bitwise() || !observation.generation().rng_state_exact() { return Err(ReferenceHandoffError::Invariant( "scalar reference handoff evidence changed", )); } Ok(ReferenceHandoffTrace { identity, digest, source_revision: source.source_revision().to_owned(), observation, }) }
What matching identities do not prove
A matching digest identifies the same canonical input record, subject to the hash’s collision-resistance assumption. It does not prove that the algorithm is correct or that a new machine will reproduce every floating-point bit.
The source identity deliberately covers the forty first-course source files, not the evolving practical crate, this chapter’s reporting wrapper or interface. Toolchain, locked dependencies and arithmetic environment are recorded separately. A matching source digest is therefore not evidence that two execution environments match. The temporary checkpoint path is also outside the input identity; changing that path does not change the model’s fixed inputs.
Likewise, exact checkpoint reload is narrower than complete job resumption. This check does not restore every data cursor, in-flight operation or whole-job continuation state. No laptop throughput is measured here.

Formula: distinguish retention from quality
For a nonempty input corpus, the final document-retention fraction is
r_{\mathrm{keep}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{prepared}}}{N_{\mathrm{input}}}

Here N_{\mathrm{input}} is the number of input document occurrences, N_{\mathrm{prepared}} is the number remaining after the declared preparation stages, and r_{\mathrm{keep}} is a dimensionless fraction. Neither count is a byte count or token count. With zero input documents, the fraction is undefined; report that condition rather than inventing a zero-quality score.
In the six-document example, quality filtering retains 4/6 of the original input. Duplicate removal retains 3/4 of its own input: the four records that reached that stage. Their product is the final retention fraction,
\frac{4}{6}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}.

Changing the denominator changes the question. Reporting 1/6 as the duplicate stage’s exclusion fraction would use the original input population rather than the 4 records the duplicate stage examined. Keep every stage’s entering and leaving document counts so its fraction can be interpreted locally.
Keeping half the input says how much remains under this policy. It does not say that half was bad, that the survivors are safe, or that a model trained on them will perform well. Those claims need different evidence.

History: more text was not the whole solution
Collecting readable text alone does not document its intended use, control the weight of repeated occurrences or protect held-out evaluation from training overlap.
Dataset documentation makes source context reviewable; deduplication studies connect repeated training text with memorization and train-test overlap in their measured settings.
Datasheets for Datasets was first posted in 2018. Gebru and colleagues propose documenting dataset motivation, composition, collection and intended uses so those choices can be reviewed. Documentation records context; it does not itself establish permission or privacy.
The 2021 C4 analysis examined where web-corpus text came from and what filtering removed. Its finding that blocklist filtering disproportionately excluded text from and about minority individuals is a reason to inspect exclusions, not to label every filter neutral.
In 2022, Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better studied duplicate handling in training corpora. Lee and colleagues report reduced memorized output and train-test overlap after deduplication in their studied corpora and models; those outcomes are not measurements of this course fixture. They explain why duplicate handling and evaluation separation matter in addition to collecting and documenting text.
The following Rust comparison loads two identical supplied records and keeps both. It illustrates the limitation of merely reading raw occurrences, not a reimplementation of those studies’ preparation tools:
Reading two identical JSONL records returns two documents; the loader does not silently perform duplicate removal. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs#loading-is-not-preparation #[test] fn loader_does_not_curate_repeated_ids_or_text() { let source = b"{\"id\":\"same\",\"text\":\"same text\"}\n{\"id\":\"same\",\"text\":\"same text\"}\n"; let documents = PreparedCorpusReader::new(Cursor::new(source), limits()) .unwrap() .collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>() .unwrap(); assert_eq!(documents.len(), 2); assert_eq!(documents[0], documents[1]); }
Keep documented source and selection evidence, inspect exclusions, handle related records together and preserve held-out roles before tokenizer learning or model training. No single preparation statistic certifies suitability.

Load the prepared output in Rust
PreparedCorpusReader accepts any caller-supplied BufRead stream. A file, memory buffer or database export can supply that stream without changing the loader. Standard buffered I/O reads physical lines; Serde JSON parses their objects. The loader preserves decoded text and metadata. It does not normalize text, reject duplicate content or assign a split.
The prepared-corpus loader uses Serde JSON to decode required document fields, then rejects blank IDs or text without rewriting their content. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs#prepared-document-json let document: PreparedDocument = serde_json::from_slice(&self.buffer) .map_err(|source| CorpusReadError::InvalidJson { line, source })?; for (field, value) in [("id", &document.id), ("text", &document.text)] { if value.trim().is_empty() { return Err(CorpusReadError::EmptyField { line, field }); } }
The caller chooses maximum source-record bytes, document count and cumulative decoded-text bytes. Record bytes include the physical line ending; decoded text bytes count the UTF-8 representation of the text value, not JSON syntax or metadata. An oversized record, malformed JSON, missing required field, failed read or exceeded limit stops the stream with an error. No failed document is returned or counted. Documents returned earlier are not rolled back.
The prepared-corpus iterator stops after successful end of input or its first error; it never resumes past a failed record. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/data/prepared_corpus.rs#prepared-corpus-stream fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> { if self.finished { return None; } match self.read_document() { Ok(Some(document)) => Some(Ok(document)), Ok(None) => { self.finished = true; None } Err(error) => { self.finished = true; Some(Err(error)) } } }
The demo reads standard input, retains only the first three document descriptions for its summary, and emits that summary only after the complete input succeeds. It can therefore inspect a large stream without retaining every text. This is not a transactional storage adapter: a caller storing documents as they arrive must provide its own staging if partial results must stay unpublished.
The Rust demo loads supplied prepared documents, reports their count and decoded text bytes, and does not repeat NeMo's preparation operations. rust/demos/practical-ch02-corpus-preparation/src/lib.rs#load-prepared-corpus pub fn summarize<R: BufRead>( source: R, limits: ReadLimits, ) -> Result<CorpusSummary, CorpusReadError> { let mut documents = PreparedCorpusReader::new(source, limits)?; let mut first_documents = Vec::with_capacity(SUMMARY_DOCUMENTS); for document in documents.by_ref() { let document = document?; if first_documents.len() < SUMMARY_DOCUMENTS { first_documents.push(DocumentSummary { id: document.id, metadata_fields: document.metadata.keys().cloned().collect(), text_utf8_bytes: document.text.len(), }); } // The tokenizer can consume document.text here. This chapter only loads // prepared records; no preparation operation is repeated inside Rust. } Ok(CorpusSummary { first_documents, loaded: documents.progress(), }) }

Practical preparation with NeMo Curator
This workflow uses a separately built NeMo Curator image. You need Linux, Docker, a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver, and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit so Docker can expose the GPU. The pinned NeMo release must be compatible with that CUDA/driver stack. Rust’s prepared-corpus reader does not require a GPU or CUDA.
Run the following commands from the repository root. The image build may use network access to obtain the external tool. It does not acquire a training corpus or add NeMo to the Rust/site image:
docker build --file docker/nemo-curator.Dockerfile \ --tag learn-llm-nemo-curator:26.07 .
With the NeMo image built and the NVIDIA GPU available to Docker, run from the repository root. Create a fresh output directory for the exercise, then run the tool with network access disabled. The read-only mount supplies the recipe and its six-record fixture; the writable mount receives generated preparation output:
mkdir -p .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture docker run --rm --network none --gpus all --memory=8g --cpus=2 --shm-size=1g \ --hostname course-nemo --add-host course-nemo:127.0.0.1 \ --mount type=bind,source="$PWD/tools/nemo-curator",target=/course,readonly \ --mount type=bind,source="$PWD/.build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture",target=/output \ learn-llm-nemo-curator:26.07 \ /course/prepare_corpus.py \ --input /course/fixtures/raw.jsonl --output /output \ --split-policy /course/fixtures/splits.json
Use an empty output directory. If the directory already contains an earlier attempt, choose a different directory rather than overwriting its evidence. The hostname mapping lets the local Ray workers resolve their container on loopback; it does not enable external network access.
The recipe invokes NeMo’s reader, configured word-count filter, exact duplicate identification and duplicate-removal workflow. Identification produces IDs to remove; it is not already the prepared text. The removal workflow must consume those IDs from the same input and ID policy, then export the remaining documents.
The filter configuration in tools/nemo-curator/prepare_corpus.py uses the library’s pipeline and stages; the recipe does not implement its own filter:
Pipeline( name="course_corpus_quality", stages=[ JsonlReader(file_paths=str(input_path), read_kwargs=read_kwargs), ScoreFilter( filter_obj=WordCountFilter(min_words=min_words, max_words=max_words, lang="en"), score_field="word_count", ), JsonlWriter(path=str(quality_path), mode="error"), ], ).run(executor=executor)
The surrounding recipe supplies the reader settings, starts a local Ray client, and runs NeMo’s exact-identification and text-removal workflows. The defaults set min_words to 3 and max_words to 20. Command-line options change those values; retain them with the output report when comparing different policies. The supplied split-policy file is independent of the observed scores.
Inspect the generated report and exported files with these commands, still from the repository root:
cat .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/report.json cat .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/prepared.jsonl cat .build/corpus/practical-ch02-exact-fixture/train.jsonl
For this fixture, the expected stage counts are 6 input documents, 4 after word-count filtering and 3 after exact duplicate removal. The final texts are A cat naps., A dog runs. and Rain feeds trees.; do not require one particular cat-story ID. The report also records one document in each role. prepared.jsonl contains all three documents for inspection; train.jsonl, validation.jsonl and test.jsonl contain their respective selections and retain the split metadata.
This is a tiny execution example with a fixed assignment of known source groups. It is not an approval of a larger corpus, a privacy check, proof that all related groups were found or a trained-model result. The helper limits input to 4 MiB and 4096 documents by default so the example is inspectable; those are not a recipe for processing the previously acquired large corpus. A bulk run needs its own feasible configuration and complete selection evidence.
For a real corpus, also retain input provenance, the tool version and configuration, excluded-document counts, the duplicate policy, split assignments and the scope of overlap and privacy review. A successful small fixture does not establish that the same resource settings fit a larger dataset. Select and measure that workload separately, preserving the raw inputs and every failed attempt.

reading.value:
The problem: the model learns from the text we let through
A language model learns to predict tokens from the documents supplied during training. Its optimizer does not decide whether those documents are appropriate for the task, whether we may use them, or whether a purportedly unseen test example also appears in the training input. Those decisions must happen before training.
Repeated text creates another problem. If one training pass visits every stored document occurrence, each copy of a document supplies another copy of its token targets. The repeated text receives more influence without adding new examples. Removing duplicates changes that weighting; it does not merely save disk space.
Corpus preparation therefore has two outputs: selected text and evidence about how it was selected. We need source context, declared exclusion rules, duplicate handling and protected evaluation boundaries. A large file or a successful download supplies none of those conclusions on its own.
We will use NVIDIA NeMo Curator to prepare text. It is an external tool, not part of the Rust language model, and another preparation tool can replace it if it produces the same documented input for the model. Rust will only load the prepared documents. The extended tokenizer in Chapter 3 will then learn from the training documents, not the validation or test documents.

reading.roleRequirement: Explain this section's stated concept, relevant inputs and operations, quantities and units, causal relationships, prerequisites, evidence and limits in the local teaching order.
reading.value:
The solution: prepare documents, then load a stable format
Keep one document as one record throughout the preparation pipeline. Retain a stable document ID and the source information needed to trace that record. A source record should identify where the text came from, its revision and the applicable license and attribution. A checksum identifies selected bytes; it does not establish permission to use those bytes or tell us what they contain.
Apply declared quality rules, inspect what those rules exclude, and handle duplicates before final training input is frozen. Quality rules are proxies: for example, a minimum word count rejects short records, not every unsuitable record. A rule can also remove useful text. Inspect both survivors and exclusions rather than interpreting a low exclusion rate as success.
Keep privacy review separate from quality scoring. Passing a word-count filter or removing duplicates does not remove names, addresses, credentials or other sensitive content. Withhold unresolved records from training; do not copy their sensitive text into public reports. Retain enough source and transformation information to identify affected derived corpora if an input is withdrawn. Removing a source from a later corpus does not erase what an already trained model may have learned from it.
A six-document example
The practical example uses course-authored text, not a result for a large training corpus. Its JSONL input contains these six documents:
Document ID | Text | Source group | Relevant observation story-a | A cat naps. | family-a | Three words story-b | A cat naps. | family-a | An identical copy of story-a story-c | A dog runs. | family-b | Three words story-d | Rain feeds trees. | family-c | Three words story-e | hi | family-e | One word story-f | !!! | family-f | Punctuation only
Configure NeMo’s word-count filter to retain records with at least 3 and at most 20 words. Its English setting counts whitespace-separated items; that proxy is not a linguistic definition of a word. The 4 story occurrences survive; hi and the punctuation-only record do not. Exact duplicate removal then leaves 3 distinct story texts. The punctuation-only record has one whitespace-separated item too; this particular rule rejects it for length, not because it recognizes punctuation as unsuitable language-model training text. The duplicate-removal workflow may retain either cat-story ID; the result we care about here is one cat-story occurrence, not a promised representative ID or output-file order.
Before deduplication, the cat story occupies 2 of the 4 surviving document occurrences. After deduplication, it occupies 1 of 3 distinct documents. Under uniform sampling of these whole-stage document occurrences before separating their roles, its selection probability would change from 2/4 to 1/3. That calculation illustrates duplicate weighting, not a sampler used to train on this fixture. Actual token-target weighting also depends on document length, split selection and the batching policy; document fractions are not token fractions.
NeMo’s exact method groups hashes of text and identifies copies to remove. It does not identify paraphrases, and hash grouping is not an adversarial collision-proof comparison. NeMo’s fuzzy method uses approximate similarity search for near-duplicates. Its configuration trades missed matches against unwanted matches; it does not certify a universal similarity cutoff or detect all ways an evaluation example could have leaked into training.
Freeze the roles of the prepared documents
The training split supplies examples for fitting the tokenizer and model. The validation split supplies examples for selecting settings or deciding when to stop training. The test split is reserved for final evaluation. Do not move a difficult held-out document into training after seeing its score.
Related records must not be scattered across those roles. Treat an identified duplicate family or other known related source group as one unit when assigning splits. Otherwise two different IDs can put substantially the same example in both training and evaluation. For this fixture, the two cat-story copies share family-a; their different IDs do not make them independent examples.
For the exercise, a supplied policy assigns family-a, family-e and family-f to training, family-b to validation and family-c to test. We fix that policy before running the filters. Both cat-story copies therefore have the same role regardless of which ID duplicate removal keeps. The prepared fixture has one document in each role: the cat story in training, the dog story in validation and the rain story in test.
The recipe uses Pandas to join those declared assignments to the source-group metadata. It refuses an unassigned group rather than choosing a convenient role after seeing the output. This checks the supplied groups, not whether we have discovered every related pair. One held-out story is also far too little evidence for a meaningful model-quality estimate.
Split disjointness and decontamination are different checks. Disjoint IDs do not prove different text. Removing exact duplicates does not prove that near-copies or external benchmark examples are absent. Declare the protected evaluation material and the overlap method before inspecting results, report its measured scope, and keep unresolved overlaps out of training. A check against a named evaluation set does not establish internet-wide contamination freedom.
Export documents, not preparation-specific objects
The handoff to Rust is UTF-8 JSON Lines: one JSON object per physical line. Each object has a nonblank string id and a nonblank string text. Other fields are retained as metadata. For example:
{"id":"story-c","text":"A dog runs.","source_group":"family-b"}
The document ID is a label, not a token ID or a required filename. The text is still text; tokenization comes next. A newline inside document text must be escaped as \n inside the JSON string, so it does not create a second record. Source and split records remain linked to the exported documents, but a JSONL file alone does not certify that those decisions were made correctly.

reading.value:
p_t=\min_{\mathrm{lex}}\operatorname*{argmax}_{(a,b)}c_t(a,b)
First collect all pairs having the largest current count. Then choose the numerically smallest pair from that set: smallest left ID, then smallest right ID. If there are no adjacent pairs, learning stops. The prepared-training policy can require an exact merge count. With that policy enabled, training fails if the documents run out of pairs before that count is reached; it does not invent vocabulary entries. Without it, the requested count is an upper limit, as in the original scalar trainer.
t is the zero-based merge rank, counting completed earlier merge rounds. a,b are the left and right content token IDs of an adjacent pair in a current training document. c_t(a,b) is the integer number of adjacent occurrences of that pair in the current training sequences at rank t; overlaps count and document boundaries never contribute. p_t is the selected pair: maximum current count, with ties resolved by the smallest left ID and then the smallest right ID.

reading.value:
BpeTrainer::train_prepared uses Chapter 2’s caller-supplied prepared-corpus reader. The caller supplies the training-only stream, its expected SHA-256 and the identity of the accepted corpus evidence. Training verifies the exact stream bytes and rejects any supplied split metadata that is not train. These checks do not discover overlap or establish rights, privacy or suitability; accepting that preparation evidence remains the caller’s responsibility.
The existing trainer keeps its scalar learning path. The new method adds a bounded working representation behind that same type; it does not define a second tokenizer. The existing BpeTokenizer still owns token layout, frozen rules, vocabulary expansions, document framing and byte decoding.

reading.roleRequirement: Explain this section's stated concept, relevant inputs and operations, quantities and units, causal relationships, prerequisites, evidence and limits in the local teaching order.
reading.value:
Each ingested byte becomes a token node with stable position, predecessor and successor links. The input text is then released. Consumed nodes retain their arena slots, so the node limit counts every ingested byte position. Node slots and pair indexes stay in memory under caller-selected bounds. Streaming input therefore does not mean constant-memory training or an external-memory algorithm.
A pair index records its current count and ordered live occurrence positions. A priority queue puts the greatest count first, using the smallest numeric pair when counts tie. Count updates can leave old queue entries behind. Each update changes a generation number; a popped entry is usable only if its count and generation still match the current pair state. A queue at its configured capacity is rebuilt from current pairs, preserving the same winner order.

reading.roleRequirement: Explain this section's stated concept, relevant inputs and operations, quantities and units, causal relationships, prerequisites, evidence and limits in the local teaching order.
reading.value: Replacing one pair removes the edge entering the left node, the selected edge, and the edge leaving the right node, when those edges exist. The merged node then supplies at most two new edges. Updating those edges immediately keeps adjacent replacements from subtracting a shared old edge twice. Ordered live positions enforce leftmost replacement; consumed overlapping occurrences vanish.

reading.roleRequirement: Explain this section's stated concept, relevant inputs and operations, quantities and units, causal relationships, prerequisites, evidence and limits in the local teaching order.
reading.value: The scalar reference reuses the original trainer’s complete learning loop: recount every current sequence, choose the winner and replace left to right. train_byte_fixture supplies the same two byte documents to that loop. The demo adapts its rules and counters into the artifact metadata used by the new path; it does not write another learning loop. Both canonical payloads and their hashes appear in the output, so their agreement can be inspected alongside the different working representations.

reading.value: Application has a different priority: the earliest learned rank among currently adjacent eligible pairs, followed by the leftmost position. The encoder rechecks adjacency and node versions before using a queued candidate, replaces that pair, and queues its new neighbors. Rules are topological: a merge’s operands already exist before that rule’s output ID is created.

reading.value:
Read chunks are transport boundaries, not token boundaries. encode_reader_bounded reads one whole bounded document before encoding; callers invoke it separately for each document. Literal text such as <|endoftext|> remains content bytes. The existing document-framing operation inserts BOS and EOS after content encoding. Byte decoding is exact; text decoding checks UTF-8 after concatenating all token fragments, since an individual token may contain only part of a UTF-8 character.
max_nodes bounds all ingested training byte positions in one training call, and byte positions in one encoded document. Bounded decoding uses that same numeric limit as the maximum reconstructed content-byte count for one document; it checks the total before allocating the output. A short token sequence can still expand into too many bytes. The existing vocabulary constructor separately bounds each token’s expansion with max_token_bytes and the sum of all content expansions with max_vocabulary_bytes.

Validation rejects unknown fields or versions, duplicate pairs, gaps, forward operands and inconsistent reduction counts. Vocabulary expansions and output serialization have explicit capacity checks.

reading.value:
Canonical payload bytes identify the learned tokenizer and its declared training lineage. Producer timestamps, local paths and machine details belong in a separate execution receipt. The two training strategies can emit equal tokenizer payload bytes while having different producer receipts. Equal vocabulary size alone does not identify the rules or their training source.
The fixture finishes with 4 content tokens over 8 input bytes: 4/8=0.5 content tokens per byte. Framing the two training documents adds 4 structural controls, which are excluded from that numerator. This is a sequence-length ratio, not trained-model quality or throughput. Zero input bytes have no tokens-per-byte ratio. Actual memory use and speed on a larger corpus require measurements of that workload; these bounded examples supply no full-corpus result.

reading.roleRequirement: Explain this section's stated concept, relevant inputs and operations, quantities and units, causal relationships, prerequisites, evidence and limits in the local teaching order.
reading.value:
A whole-word vocabulary leaves rare and unseen words difficult to represent; learned subwords reduce that problem, but their alphabet and boundary rules still determine which merges are possible.
In 2016, Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units introduced BPE subword learning for neural translation. Sennrich and colleagues learn subword units by repeatedly merging frequent symbol pairs, with word boundaries retained in their character-based representation. That representation is different from treating a complete document as one raw-byte sequence.
The published GPT-2 encoder applies a reversible byte-to-Unicode mapping, an explicit pretokenization pattern and ranked merges within each resulting piece. The pretokenization boundaries determine where a learned merge can apply. Inspect the pinned encoder implementation. The Unicode symbols represent bytes; the mapping does not normalize the input text.

reading.roleRequirement: Explain this section's stated concept, relevant inputs and operations, quantities and units, causal relationships, prerequisites, evidence and limits in the local teaching order.
reading.value: Our chapter-local Rust example implements the published byte mapping and pretokenization pattern. It reuses the course tokenizer’s existing frozen-rank engine inside each piece, with one hypothetical merge of a followed by 1. This isolates boundary behavior without implementing BPE again. The demo’s tiny vocabulary defines its displayed IDs; they are not the pretrained GPT-2 vocabulary’s IDs.

reading.value: The raw-byte fixture learns a1 from a1a1 and encodes a1 as one content token. The published GPT-2 pattern splits a1 into the letter piece a and the digit piece 1 before BPE. The proposed merge cannot cross those pieces, so this policy example emits two content tokens. Both paths reconstruct the same input bytes. Reconstruction therefore does not imply equal segmentation.

reading.value:
The regex engine executes the fixed published pattern; Rust owns the byte map, the existing rank decisions and the illustrative vocabulary IDs. The byte map is reversible and does not create a merge across separate pieces. Here the rank engine works on the pieces’ raw bytes; the resulting byte fragments are then expressed through the map and tiny vocabulary. This demonstrates selected published operations rather than reproducing the pretrained tokenizer. Its bounded results do not establish agreement with every behavior of the original Python regex runtime.
Freeze the training selection and tokenizer policy before constructing decoder token targets. Improve the implementation without changing those learned decisions or confusing byte reconstruction with equal segmentation.

reading.value: The count tables refer to the representation immediately before each rank. They change after replacement. The scalar and incremental course paths reach the same learned payload; the letter-digit example changes the boundary policy and consequently the eligible merges.

reading.value: Use the frozen course tokenizer to encode each prepared document separately. Held-out encoding does not fit new merges. Chapter 4 will place those token sequences into variable-length batches without changing tokenizer identity. The embedding and output layers must continue to interpret each content ID according to that same learned vocabulary.

reading.roleRequirement: Explain this section's stated concept, relevant inputs and operations, quantities and units, causal relationships, prerequisites, evidence and limits in the local teaching order.
reading.value:
Our byte-pair encoding trainer counts adjacent token pairs, selects one pair, replaces its occurrences and repeats. The first course’s Chapter 3 implemented that scalar trainer; Chapter 4 applied its frozen ranks and decoded the resulting tokens. Both are already in the practical course’s starting crate. Here we extend the existing BpeTrainer and BpeTokenizer.
The scalar trainer recounts every current training sequence at every merge rank. With more documents and more requested merges, those repeated scans revisit many edges that have not changed.
We can retain pair statistics and update the edges affected by a replacement. Local updates avoid recounting unaffected edges, but introduce a correctness obligation: the retained counts must describe the current sequences exactly. An old count or an out-of-order replacement can change the learned vocabulary even if the result still decodes to the original bytes.
We will preserve the course’s policy: learn from training documents only, count overlapping adjacent occurrences, break frequency ties by numeric token IDs, and replace matches left to right without sharing an input token between two replacements. A faster implementation of that policy must keep those decisions.

reading.roleRequirement: Explain this section's stated concept, relevant inputs and operations, quantities and units, causal relationships, prerequisites, evidence and limits in the local teaching order.
reading.value:
Use two manually prepared training documents, abab and abac. They are separate documents, so the last byte of one never forms a pair with the first byte of the other. The held-out text acac will be encoded after learning; it supplies no pair counts.
Keep the existing public token layout. Program IDs 0 and 1 are BOS and EOS; one-byte content IDs run from 2 through 257. The bytes a, b and c therefore have IDs 99, 100 and 101. The first learned content ID is 258. There is no PAD token. BOS and EOS are structural controls and do not enter training pair counts.
Before rank 0, the current sequences are [99,100,99,100] and [99,100,99,101]. The pair a,b occurs 3 times, b,a occurs 2 times, and a,c occurs once. Select a,b, assign its merged bytes ab the new ID 258, and replace its nonoverlapping occurrences. The sequences become [258,258] and [258,99,101].
Before rank 1, there are only three adjacent occurrences: (258,258), (258,99) and (99,101), each with count 1. Numeric pair order compares the left IDs first. The pair (99,101) wins the tie, so the bytes ac receive ID 259. The two training sequences are now [258,258] and [258,259].
The frozen rules encode held-out acac as [259,259]. Decoding those content tokens reconstructs acac; document framing would instead give [0,259,259,1]. Encoding held-out text applies the learned rules and does not learn another rule.

reading.value: The existing BPE trainer accepts bounded prepared documents and delegates local pair updates to its private working representation. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/tokenizer/bpe_trainer.rs#bounded-prepared-training /// Extend this trainer to bounded, selected prepared documents with local pair updates. pub fn train_prepared<R: std::io::Read>( self, reader: R, read_limits: crate::data::prepared_corpus::ReadLimits, binding: super::policy::TrainingBinding, policy: super::policy::TokenizerPolicy, limits: super::policy::TokenizerLimits, trace: bool, ) -> Result<PreparedBpeTraining, super::policy::TokenizerError> { if self.max_merges != policy.merge_count { return Err(super::policy::TokenizerError::Policy( "trainer and serialized merge budgets differ", )); } super::incremental::train_prepared(reader, read_limits, binding, policy, limits, trace) }

reading.value: Choose the greatest current pair count with the course's numeric tie rule; discard queue entries invalidated by later count updates. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/tokenizer/incremental.rs#incremental-pair-choice fn winner(&mut self) -> Option<(TokenPair, u64)> { while let Some(entry) = self.heap.pop() { let pair = entry.pair.0; if self.pairs.get(&pair).is_some_and(|state| { state.count == entry.count && state.generation == entry.generation }) { return Some((pair, entry.count)); } } None }

reading.roleRequirement: Relate the displayed Rust operation, its actual caption and source locator to the computation or evidence this example supplies, with consistent inputs, operations and stated scope.
reading.value: Visit leftmost live matches, remove disappearing edges once and add the new neighboring edges after each replacement. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch-practical/src/tokenizer/incremental.rs#local-edge-replacement fn replace(&mut self, pair: TokenPair, output: u32) -> Result<u64, TokenizerError> { let mut replacements = 0u64; // Stable indices follow source order; first() gives the leftmost live match. while let Some(left) = self .pairs .get(&pair) .and_then(|s| s.occurrences.first()) .copied() { if self.edge(left) != Some(pair) { return Err(TokenizerError::Invariant("stale live occurrence")); } let right = self.nodes[left] .next .ok_or(TokenizerError::Invariant("pair has no right node"))?; let previous = self.nodes[left].previous; let next = self.nodes[right].next; // Three distinct edge starts disappear; adjacent replacements cannot // remove a shared old edge twice because the lists update immediately. if let Some(index) = previous { self.remove_edge(index)?; } self.remove_edge(left)?; self.remove_edge(right)?; self.nodes[left].token = output; self.nodes[left].next = next; self.nodes[right].alive = false; if let Some(index) = next { self.nodes[index].previous = Some(left); } if let Some(index) = previous { self.add_edge(index)?; } self.add_edge(left)?; replacements = replacements .checked_add(self.weights[self.nodes[left].document]) .ok_or(TokenizerError::Overflow)?; } Ok(replacements) }

|| self.counters.content_tokens > self.counters.input_bytes { return Err(TokenizerError::Artifact("inconsistent efficiency counters")); } let layout = TokenizerLayout::new(self.merges.len())?; let mut pairs = Vec::new(); pairs .try_reserve_exact(self.merges.len()) .map_err(|_| TokenizerError::Resource("merge operand allocation failed"))?; let mut reduction = 0u64; for (rank, rule) in self.merges.iter().enumerate() { if rule.rank != rank || layout.merge_token_id(rank) != Some(rule.token_id) || rule.replacements == 0 || rule.replacements > rule.candidate_count { return Err(TokenizerError::Artifact("invalid rank or merge count")); } let left = rule .left .checked_sub(CONTENT_ID_OFFSET) .ok_or(TokenizerError::Artifact( "control ID cannot be a merge operand", ))?; let right = rule.right .checked_sub(CONTENT_ID_OFFSET) .ok_or(TokenizerError::Artifact( "control ID cannot be a merge operand", ))?; pairs.push(TokenPair::new(left, right)); reduction = reduction .checked_add(rule.replacements) .ok_or(TokenizerError::Overflow)?; } if self.counters.input_bytes.checked_sub(reduction) != Some(self.counters.content_tokens) { return Err(TokenizerError::Artifact( "merge reductions disagree with content count", )); } // This single constructor owns prior-rank operands, duplicate pairs, // byte expansions and their bounds; there is no second vocabulary here. Ok(BpeTokenizer::from_merge_pairs_bounded( &pairs, limits.max_token_bytes, limits.max_vocabulary_bytes, )?) }

reading.value: Map each possible byte to a reversible Unicode symbol and define the chapter's illustrative vocabulary IDs. rust/demos/practical-ch03-scalable-bpe-tokenizer/src/gpt2_contrast.rs#gpt2-byte-mapping let mut byte_order = (b'!'..=b'~') .chain(0xa1..=0xac) .chain(0xae..=0xff) .collect::<Vec<_>>(); let mut symbols = byte_order .iter() .map(|&byte| char::from(byte)) .collect::<Vec<_>>(); let mut next_codepoint = 256u32; for byte in 0..=255u8 { if !byte_order.contains(&byte) { let symbol = char::from_u32(next_codepoint).ok_or("invalid byte-map symbol")?; byte_order.push(byte); symbols.push(symbol); next_codepoint += 1; } } let mut bytes = ['\0'; 256]; let mut reverse_bytes = BTreeMap::new(); let mut vocabulary = BTreeMap::new(); for (id, (&byte, &symbol)) in byte_order.iter().zip(&symbols).enumerate() { bytes[byte as usize] = symbol; reverse_bytes.insert(symbol, byte); vocabulary.insert(symbol.to_string(), id as u32); }

# Chapter 0: The structure of Practical LLM in Rust

<!-- contract-section:scope -->
## Scope

Orientation only: identify the independent copied implementation, prerequisites,
initial material and later roadmap. Do not introduce a second algorithm, formula
lesson, Rust implementation sample, exercise, answer or cheat sheet.

<!-- contract-section:overview -->
## Orientation commitments

The practical crate starts from the restored first-course implementation and is
evolved independently. First-course lessons and algorithms stay unchanged.
Chapter 1 records the fixed baseline experiment; Chapter 2 separates external
preparation from Rust loading; Chapter 3 extends the existing BPE implementation.
Available links must correspond to published practical chapters. If Chapter 3
is pending at the foundation checkpoint, show its named role as roadmap text
until its complete chapter is published.

<!-- contract-section:history -->
## Starting point

The historical comparison for this orientation is course-local: building small
mechanisms first, then extending the completed model. Make no new primary-source
historical claim and reuse no first-course diagram as a new taught mechanism.

<!-- contract-section:course-path -->
## Chapter sequence

Give each initial chapter its concrete purpose: identified reference inputs and
scope, external preparation and Rust loading, then extension of existing BPE.
Link available practical Chapters 1, 2 and 3, keeping each chapter's concrete purpose next to its link. Link the
course index for current availability. Explain the subsequent batching, model
configuration, GPU, training, resume, evaluation, adaptation, inference and
serving stages as a roadmap rather than completed measurements.

<!-- contract-section:visualization -->
## Navigation evidence

An ordered list supplies the chapter-to-purpose mapping. No figure is required.
Explain that concrete reason without referring to rendering or build machinery.

<!-- contract-section:decoder-connection -->
## Practical path

Keep one causal text model as the subject. Distinguish small examples from
full-corpus or hardware measurements. CPU reference and loading of prepared
documents remain available; the GPU-backed path and external NeMo stack require
a compatible NVIDIA device and driver.

<!-- contract-section:localization -->
## Locale scope

Practical lessons are English only, including order zero; locale configuration
and future activation remain supported. Russian home may link explicitly to the
English practical destination. No Russian practical lesson is emitted.

<!-- contract-section:acceptance -->
## Acceptance

Scoped orientation schema, no cheat sheet, static links and locale semantics,
English independent reviews and adjudications, and sole-Firefox desktop/narrow
containment and navigation. The foundation checkpoint retains pending full-data
preparation and hardware gates; small fixtures do not discharge them.
